articles.title: खल्तीबाट डिजिटल भुक्तानी गर्दा दैनिक १ लाख र बम्परमा १० लाख जित्न सकिने
articles.summary:
काठमाडौँ । आईएमई खल्ती लिमिटेडले अर्थ मन्त्रालयअन्तर्गतको आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागद्वारा सञ्चालित ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम, २०८३’ मा आफ्ना प्रयोगकर्तालाई सहभागी गराउने भएको छ। खल्तीमार्फत रु १०० भन्दा बढीको योग्य डिजिटल भुक्तानी गर्दा ग्राहकहरू स्वतः दैनिक तथा पाक्षिक उपहार छनोटमा सहभागी हुनेछन्।

यस कार्यक्रमअन्तर्गत दैनिक एक जना विजेताले कर कट्टीपछि रु. १ लाख र प्रत्येक १५ दिनमा एक जना बम्पर विजेताले रु १० लाख प्राप्त गर्नेछन्। भुक्तानीको विवरण सुरक्षित रूपमा राजस्व विभागको प्रणालीमा पुग्ने र उपहार कुपन स्वतः सिर्जना भई खल्ती एपमै देखिने व्यवस्था मिलाइएको छ। विभागले प्रत्येक महिनाको १ र १६ गते स्वचालित प्रणालीबाट विजेता छनोट गरी एसएमएस, इमेल तथा खल्तीमार्फत जानकारी गराउनेछ।

बिलमा आधारित कारोबार प्रवर्द्धन गरी डिजिटल अर्थतन्त्र र राष्ट्रिय राजस्व प्रणालीलाई सुदृढ बनाउने लक्ष्यका साथ यो सहकार्य गरिएको आईएमई खल्तीका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत प्रवीण रेग्मीले बताएका छन्।

articles.title: सर्वसाधारणको रकम गरिमा विकास बैंकले झ्वाम पार्दै, झ्वाम पार्ने को–को ?
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । के तपाईंको गरिमा विकास बैंकमा खाता छ ?के तपाईंले आफुले मेहेनत गरेको रकम गरिमा बिकास बैंकमा राख्नु भएको छ ? यदी छ भने तपाईंका लागि आज दुखको खबर छ । कारण हो, ग्राहकले राखेको रकम बैंकको भवन किन्दा अपचलन गरेर प्रचलित मूल्यभन्दा बढी मूल्यामा किनिएको छ । प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदन र प्रचलित बजार मूल्यलाई समेत लत्याउँदै बैंक व्यवस्थापनले ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्य तिरेको छ । सर्वसाधारणले दुःख गरेर बैंकमा जम्मा गरेको निक्षेप सुरक्षित छ त?भन्ने प्रश्न पनि उठिरहेको छ ।

गरिमा विकास बैंकले काठमाडौँको बालुवाटारमा ३७ आनाभन्दा बढी जग्गा र त्यसमा बनेको घर खरिद गर्दा प्रचलित बजार मूल्य र स्वयं प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदनलाई समेत लत्याउँदै करिब ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्य तिरिएको भेटिएको छ। बजार मन्दीमा रहेका बेला प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन भन्दा दोब्बर मूल्य हालेर जग्गा र भवन किनिएको छ ।

काठमाडौंको बालुवाटारमा कित्ता नम्बर ४९ मा रहेको २ रोपनी ५ आना १ पैसा अर्थात् ३७ दशमलव २६ आना जग्गा र ४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिटको बनेको यो आरसीसी भवन शिखर इन्स्योरेन्सका पूर्वअध्यक्ष राजेन्द्रप्रसाद श्रेष्ठको २०८२ सालमा गरिमा विकास बैंकले केन्द्रीय कार्यालय बनाउन खरिद ग¥यो ।

बैंकले यो जग्गा खरिद गर्दा प्रतिआना १ करोड ५६ लाख १४ हजार ९२२ रुपैयाँ तिरेको देखिन्छ । अर्थात २ रोपनी ५ आना १ पैसाको जग्गाको मूल्या ५८ करोड १८ लाख १२ हजार रुपैयाँ बैकलाई पर्न गयो। अब यही जग्गामा रहेको यो भवनको क्षेत्रफल ४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिट रहेको छ ।

बैंकले यो भवनको मूल्य ३९ करोड ३१ लाख ८८ हजार रुपैयाँमा खरिद गरेको देखिन्छ । वर्गफिटमा हिसाब गर्दा पनि प्रति वर्गफिट ८ हजार २ सय ५६ रुपैयाँमा खरिद गरको छ । तपाईलाई यो खरिद मूल्य सायद सामान्य नै लाग्यो होला? यो सामान्य घरजग्गा किनबेच देखिए तापनि, प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन र बैंकको हालेको रकम जुधाउँदा भने ठूलो अन्तर देखिन्छ ।

प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन र बजार मूल्यको वास्तविकता

पृथक इन्जिनियरिङ कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले बैंक धितोकै लागि तयार पारेको प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदन अनुसार सो क्षेत्रमा जग्गाको स्थानीय बजार दर प्रतिआना ८० लाख रुपैयाँ मात्र छ। स्थानीय व्यवसायीहरूका अनुसार पनि बजारको अधिकतम मूल्य ९० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी पर्दैन।

प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदनमा सडकको अधिकार क्षेत्र कट्टा गरी कायम भएको १ रोपनी १३ आना ३ पैसा जग्गाको कुल बजार मूल्य १७ करोड ७० लाख ९८ हजार मात्रै कायम गरेको छ । पृथक इन्जिनियरिङ कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले कमर्सियल भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भनेको २३ करोड ८३ लाख ९९ हजार यो जग्गाको मूल्या कायम गरेको छ । फेयर मार्केट भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भनेको १७ करोड ७० लाख ९८ हजार कायम गर्यो ।

डिस्ट्रेस भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भने १४ करोड १६ लाख ७८ हजार कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले कायम गरेको छ । तर बंैकले बैंकले भने सोही जग्गालाई ५८ करोड १८ लाखभन्दा बढी भुक्तानी गर्यो। यो खेल जग्गामा मात्र रोकिएन, भवन खरिदमा पनि उस्तै अस्वाभाविक मूल्या हालियो ।

४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिट क्षेत्रफल रहेको सो भवनको मूल्य बैंकले ३९ करोड ३१ लाख ८८ हजार रुपैयाँ तय गरेर खरिद ग¥यो। अर्थात् प्रतिवर्गफिट ८ हजार २ सय ५६ रुपैयाँ! निर्माण व्यवसायीहरूका अनुसार काठमाडौँमा अत्यन्त लक्जरियस सामग्री प्रयोग गर्दा पनि नयाँ भवन निर्माण खर्च प्रतिवर्गफिट अधिकतम ४ हजारदेखि ६ हजार रुपैयाँसम्म मात्र पुग्छ। प्रतिवर्गफिट ६ हजार नै मान्ने हो भने पनि २८ करोड ५७ लाख पर्ने भवनलाई बैंकले १० करोड ७४ लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी अतिरिक्त मूल्य हालेर किनेको देखिन्छ ।

जग्गामा २४ करोड ६५ लाख र घरमा १० करोड ७४ लाख गरी कुल ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी रकम बजार मूल्य र प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कनभन्दा बढी मूल्य हालिएको छ । घर–जग्गा बजारमा मन्दी छाएका बेला प्रचलित भाउभन्दा निकै माथि गएर गरिएको यो निर्णयमा गरिमा विकास बैंकका सञ्चालक अनिल रेग्मी, ईश्वरीप्रसाद ढकाल र सीईओ माधवप्रसाद उपाध्याय लगायतको भूमिका देखिन्छ ।

सर्वसाधारण निक्षेपकर्ताको पसिनाको कमाईमाथि बैंकका सञ्चालक र उच्च व्यवस्थापनबाट भएको यो अस्वाभाविक खर्चले बैंकको संस्थागत सुशासन र नियमनकारी निकाय नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकको अनुगमनमाथि ठूलो प्रश्न खडा गरेको छ।

articles.title: फोनिज काठमाडौँको आयोजनामा वृक्षरोपण तथा पदयात्रा सम्पन्न
articles.summary:
काठमाडौँ । नेपाल आदिवासी जनजाति पत्रकार महासंघ (फोनिज) काठमाडौँ जिल्ला कार्यसमितिको आयोजनामा वृक्षरोपण तथा फोनिज पदयात्रा सम्पन्न भएको छ ।

फोनिजको २७ औँ स्थापना दिवसको अवसर पारेर आज शनिवार काठमाडौँको साँखु–बज्रयोगिनी हुँदै मणिचूड दहसम्म पदयात्रा तथा विभिन्न गुम्बा तथा मन्दिर परिसरमा वृक्षरोपण गरेका हुन् । काठमाडौँ जिल्ला अन्तरगत फोनिज आवद्ध प्रतिनिधिहरू, स्थानीय जनप्रतिनिधि र विभिन्न जातिय संघसंस्थाका प्रतिनिधिहरूको उल्लेख्य सहभागितामा साँखुमा भेला भइ बज्रयोगिनी मन्दिर परिसरबाट करिव १७ किलोमिटिरको दूरीमा पदयात्रा गरेका थिए ।

पदयात्रापछि मणिचूड दहमा भएको औपचारिक कार्यक्रममा विभिन्न वक्ताहरूले धार्मिक पर्यटन प्रवद्र्धन र संरक्षणमा आदिवासी जनजातिहरूको महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका रहेको बताएका छन् । कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै शंकरापुर नगरपालिका वडा नं. ८ का अध्यक्ष पोते थिङले मणिचूड दहको महत्वबारे प्रकाश पार्दै प्रचारप्रसारको अभाव तथा राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्ज वन क्षेत्रको निश्चित मापदण्डका कारण अझै ओझेलमा परेको बताए । मणिचूड दह र त्यस क्षेत्रमा रहेका हरेक धार्मिक तथा साँस्कृतिक सम्पदाको संरक्षण र प्रवद्र्धनका साथै थप व्यवस्थापन गर्न वनसंग जोडिएको कानुनलाई परिमार्जण गर्नुपर्ने धारणा राखे ।

त्यस्तै शिवपुरी नागार्जुन राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्ज मध्यवर्ती क्षेत्र व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष श्यामकुमार वाइबाले निकुञ्जभित्र रहेको मणिचूड दह बौद्ध र हिन्दू दुवै धर्मालम्बीहरू पवित्र तिर्थस्थलको रूपमा मान्दै आएको बताए । विशेष गरि जनजातिजातिको बहुल्यता रहेको त्यस क्षेत्रमा बौद्ध धर्मालम्बीहरूले विभिन्न समयमा पूजापाठ, मोन्लाम लगायत साउन महिने जलयात्रा, जनैपूर्णिमा लगायत साँस्कृतिक पर्वहरू मनाउने भएकोले थप महत्व रहेको बताए । अहिले निकुञ्ज, स्थानीय तह र मन्दिर व्यवस्थापन समितिबीचको समन्वयमा व्यवस्थित बनाउने रणनीति रहेको बताए ।

कार्यक्रममा राष्ट्रि शहिद तथा शान्ति स्मारक पार्क र गोकर्ण यज्ञडोल सामुदायिक वन उपभोक्त समितिका अध्यक्ष सुर्दशन सिग्देलले वन, जंगल, जल र जमिनको संरक्षणमा जनजाति समुदायको उल्लेख्य भूमिका रहेको बताउँदै आफ्नो साँस्कृतिक पहिचान र अधिकारसँग जाडिएको क्षेत्रमा राज्यले दुःख दिन नहुने बताए । जनजाति समुदायले विशेष गरि प्रकृतिको पुजा गर्ने चाडपर्वलाई साँस्कृतिक पहिचानको रूपमा विश्वमाझ चिनाउन सफल रहेको बताउँदै राष्ट्रिय शहिद पार्क वन क्षेत्रमा समेत विभन्नि जातजातिको अस्तित्व समेट्ने गरि भिलेजग्रामको निर्माण गरिएको बताए ।

फोनिज बागमति प्रदेश समितिका महासचिव राजु नापितले फोनिजले पत्रकारितालाई आफ्नो पेसागत हकअधिकारमात्र नभएर भाषा, कला, संस्कृतिको संरक्षण र सम्वद्र्धनमा विशेष योगदान पु¥याउँदै आइरहेको बताए । फोनिज बागमति प्रदेशभित्र पत्रकारहरूलाई एकीकृत गराउँदै समुदायको पहिचान र अधिकार सुनिश्चित गराउन समेत जिल्लासमितिहरूले सक्रियतापूर्वक गतिविधि सञ्चालन गराउँदै आएको बताए ।

त्यस्तै फोनिज संघीय समितिका सचिव सुनिल महर्जनले फोनिज पदयात्राले रमाइलो मात्र नभइ अनुसन्धानका आयाम बुझ्न पाएको बताए । मणिचूडको सुन्दर ऐतिहासिक धार्मिक पर्यटकीय स्थल प्रकृतिप्रेमी र आध्यात्मिक शान्ति चाहनेहरूका लागि विशेष रहने बताउँदै पत्रकारिताको माध्यमबाट प्रचारप्रसारलाई तिब्रता दिनुपर्ने बताए । फोनिजले नेपालभित्र रहेका आदिवासी जनजाति समुदायसंग जोडिएका कला, भाषा, धर्म संस्कृति र पहिचान बोकेका विषयवस्तुहरूको अध्ययन र अनुसन्धान गरि विश्वसामु चिनाउने प्रयास गरिरहेको बताए ।

नेपाल आदिवासी जनजाति पत्रकार महासंघ (फोनिज) काठमाडौँ जिल्ला समितिका अध्यक्ष भिमबहादुर लामाले सामाजिक एकता र सद्भाव कायम उद्देश्यका साथ फोनिजको २७ औँ स्थापना दिवसलाई सार्थक पार्न पदयात्रा तथा वृक्षरोपण कार्यक्रमको आयोजना गरिएको बताए । उनले जनजाति पत्रकारहरूको पेसागत क्षमतालाई दरिलो बनाउन अध्ययन, अनुसन्धान र आलेख लेखनमा सहयोग पु¥याउने उद्देश्यले धार्मिक पर्यटकीय क्षेत्र तथा जनजाति समुदायको साँस्कृतिक तथा धार्मिक महत्व बोकेको क्षेत्र साँखु, बज्रयोगिनी र मणिचूड दहको यात्रा तय गरेको बताए । राज्य र पहुँचवाला समूहहरूबाट आदिवासी जनजातिहरूको थातथालोमा जलविद्युत गुरूयोजनाहरू सञ्चालन गर्ने, विकास निर्माण र राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्जको नाममा परिवारहरू विस्थापित बनाएको अध्यक्ष लामाले आरोप लगाए ।

फोनिज काठमाडौँ जिल्ला कार्यसमितिका सचिव रत्नमान महर्जनले सञ्चालन गरेको कार्यक्रममा नेपाल प्रहरीका पूर्व डिआइजी देउती गुरूङ, गोकर्णेश्वर नगरपालिका वडा नं. ८ का वडा सदस्य सुमन लामा, नेपाल पत्रकार महासंघ काठमाडौँ शाखा उपाध्यक्षद्वाय कमल राना मगर, कान्ति न्यौपाने, सहसचिब बिक्रम रत्न, मणिचूड मन्दिर व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष भिम घ्लान, नेपाल बौद्ध धर्म संरक्षण संघका महासचिव उमा गुरूङ, साँस्कृतिक युवा समूहका अध्यक्ष वेचन लामा, समाजसेवी किरण मोक्तान, सोफिया पाख्रिन लगायत अतिथि रहेका थिए । पदयात्रामा फोनिजकर्मी तथा विभिन्न संघसंस्थाका प्रतिनिधि गरि ६८ जनाको सहभागीता रहेको थियो ।

articles.title: हेटौँडामा पर्यटन वर्षको बहारः ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । बाग्मती प्रदेशको राजधानी हेटौँडामा पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ लाई लक्षित गर्दै ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान सञ्चालन गरिएको छ । ‘जाऔँ हेटौंडा, रमाऔँ हेटौंडामा’ भन्ने मूल नारासहित मनाइन लागिएको पर्यटन वर्ष २०८३ को पहिलो र प्रमुख कार्यक्रमका रूपमा ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान अन्तर्गत सरसफाइ थालिएको हो ।

यो वर्ष बाग्मतीको प्रादेशिक राजधानीस्थित हेटौँडा उपमहानगरपालिकाले पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ मनाउँदैछ । पर्यटन वर्षको कार्यक्रम अन्तर्गत सून्य फोहोर अभियान सञ्चालन गरिएको छ । यहि अभियान अन्तर्गत शनिवार हातमा कुचो र बोरा बोकेर जनप्रतिनिधि, सुरक्षाकर्मी, टोल विकास संस्थाका पदाधिकारी र स्थानीयवासी सडकमा निस्किए । हेटौँडाका सडकदेखि टोलसम्म सरसफाइ गर्दै उनीहरूले ‘शून्य फोहोर हेटौँडा’ अभियान शुरु गरेका हुन् ।

फोहोर व्यवस्थापनलाई केवल सरसफाइ अभियानका रूपमा नभई पर्यटन, वातावरण संरक्षण र नागरिक संस्कृतिसँग जोडिएको दीर्घकालीन अभियानका रूपमा अघि बढाइने योजना उपमहानगरपालिकाको छ । उपमहानगरपालिकाले ‘जाऔँ हेटौंडा, रमाऔँ हेटौंडामा’ भन्ने मूल नारासहित मनाइने पर्यटन वर्ष २०८३ को पहिलो र प्रमुख कार्यक्रमका रूपमा ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान अघि सारिएको हो ।

मुख्य तथा सहायक सडक, सार्वजनिक स्थल र पर्यटकीय क्षेत्रको सरसफाइसँगै वृक्षारोपण र सौन्दर्यीकरणलाई पनि अभियानको प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ । टोल विकास संस्था नगर समन्वय समितिको संयोजनमा सुरु भएको अभियान नगरका ३ सय ७७ वटै टोल विकास संस्थामा सुरु गरिएको छ । पर्यटन वर्षको अवसरमा सुरु गरिएको ‘शून्य फोहोर हेटौँडा’ अभियानले नगरको स्वच्छता र सौन्दर्य कायम राख्दै हेटौँडालाई पर्यटकीय गन्तव्यका रूपमा चिनाउन सहयोग पुग्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको दाबी छ ।

पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ मा हेटौँडामा आन्तरिक तथा बाह्य पर्यटकको संख्या बढाउने उपमहानगरपालिकाको लक्ष्य छ । पर्यटकलाई आकर्षित गर्न नयाँ गन्तव्यको प्रचारसँगै शहरको स्वच्छता, सौन्दर्य र व्यवस्थित वातावरणलाई पनि प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ ।

यही उद्देश्यले सुरु गरिएको यो अभियानलाई नगरका ३ सय ७७ वटै टोलसम्म विस्तार गरिँदैछ । टोल–टोलमा सरसफाइ र फोहोर व्यवस्थापनलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउँदै हेटौँडालाई स्वच्छ, सुन्दर र पर्यटकमैत्री शहरका रूपमा विकास गर्ने र पर्यटन वर्षमा बढीभन्दा बढी पर्यटक भित्र्याउने लक्ष्य लिइएको छ ।

articles.title: इन्सेन्टिभ वितरण नहुँदा सेवा ठप्प, मर्कामा सर्वसाधारण विरामी
articles.summary:
महोत्तरी । प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरमा सेवा लिन आउने नागरिक अनाहकमा पिडित बन्न पुगेका छन । मेडिकल सुपिरिटेंडेन्ट, अस्पताल संचालन तथा व्यस्थापन् समिति अध्यक्ष बिचको तालमेल समस्या र भिडियो एक्सरे गर्ने स्वास्थ्यकर्मीको बाकी इन्सेन्टिभ जस्ता आन्तरिक विवादका कारण सेवाग्राहीलाई मर्का परिरहेको छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरमा अस्पतालमा भिडियो एक्सरे सेवा बन्द भएपछि बिरामीहरू निजी स्वास्थ्य संस्थामा महँगो शुल्क तिरेर सेवा लिन बाध्य छन् । अस्पताल प्रशासनले प्राविधिक कारणले सेवा वन्द रहेको सूचना टॉस गरि सेवा अवरुद्ध रहेको बताएको छ । तर भित्री कुरा भने भिडियो एक्सरे गर्ने चिकित्सकलाई इन्सेन्टिभ उपलब्ध नगराइएका कारण सो सेवा विगत दुई हप्ताभन्दा बढी समयदेखि वन्द रहेको छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरका निमित्त कार्यालय प्रमुख डा.रवि श्रीवास्तवले इन्सेन्टिभकै समस्याको कारणले दुईहप्ताभन्दा बढी समयदेखि भिडियो एक्सरे सेवा सुचारू हुन नसकेको स्विकारे । आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२\०८३ मा चिकित्सकहरुलाई इन्सेन्टिभ नदिएका कारण सेवा वन्द गरेको बताउदै समस्या समाधानको पहल गरिरहेको निमित्त कार्यालय प्रमुख डा.रवि श्रीवास्तवको भनाइ छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरका अस्पताल सञ्चालन तथा व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष रोहित प्रसाद ठाकुरले पनि काम गर्ने चिकित्सकहरुलाई इन्सेन्टिभ नदिएकै कारणले सेवा अवरुद्ध भएको बताए । उनले सेवा सुचारुको पहल गरिरहेको बताउदै अस्पताल व्यवस्थापन समितिको जेठ २८ गते बसेको बैठकले इन्सेन्टिभ दिने निर्णय गरेपनि सो किन वितरण गरिएन ? आशंका छन् ।

स्वास्थ सेवा जस्तो संवेदनशील संस्थाले अस्पतालको आन्तरिक तथा प्रशासनिक समस्याकै कारण सेवा ठप्प पार्नु, आम नागरिकलाई अनाहकमा समस्या दिनु स्वभाविक रुपमा लिन सकिदैन्। तर, यसको समाधान कसरी होला? सर्वसाधारणले नै सोध्न थालेका छन् ।

articles.title: देश धान्ने क्षेत्रमै संकट, श्रमिक विदेश पठाउन बन्द !
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । वैदेशिक रोजगारीबाट आउने रेमिट्यान्सले देशको अर्थतन्त्र धान्न सहयोग पु¥याइरहेका म्यानपावर व्यवसायीले सरकारविरुद्ध दबाब बढाएका छन् । १५ बुँदे माग अघि सार्दै नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले शुक्रवारदेखि वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द गर्ने घोषणा गरेको छ । व्यवसायीहरूले नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म कामदार नपठाउने अडान लिएका छन् ।

नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार क्षेत्रका नीतिगत समस्या समाधान नभएको भन्दै शुक्रवारदेखि श्रमिक विदेश पठाउने कार्य पूर्ण रूपमा स्थगित गरेको छ । काठमाडौँमा पत्रकार सम्मेलन गर्दै संघले रेमिट्यान्सले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा ठूलो योगदान पु¥याए पनि सरकारले समयानुकूल नीति सुधार नगर्दा व्यवसायी र श्रमिक दुवै प्रभावित भएको जनाएको छ ।

संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार ऐन–२०६४ लाई समयसापेक्ष संशोधन, पारदर्शी लागत निर्धारण, वैज्ञानिक सेवा शुल्क, श्रमिक लक्षित गन्तव्य मुलुकको हवाई भाडा घटाउने तथा कृत्रिम अभाव अन्त्य गर्न माग गरेको छ । युरोपका नयाँ श्रम बजार, दक्षिण कोरियाको ई–सेभेन भिसा, जापानको ईएसडी कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन, महिला घरेलु कामदारका लागि नयाँ गन्तव्य खुला गर्ने र विभिन्न मुलुकमा देखिएका प्रशासनिक तथा बिचौलिया समस्या कूटनीतिक पहलमार्फत समाधान गर्नुपर्ने माग पनि अघि सारिएको छ ।

संघले मागपत्र प्रमाणीकरण र श्रम स्वीकृतिलाई पूर्ण रूपमा स्वचालित बनाउन, ५ हजारभन्दा बढी नेपाली श्रमिक रहेका मुलुकमा श्रम सहचारी तथा काउन्सिलर नियुक्त गर्न, व्यवसायीले राखेको धरौटीको ब्याज उपलब्ध गराउन र श्रमिकलाई बिना धितो सहुलियतपूर्ण कर्जा दिने व्यवस्था गर्न पनि सरकारसँग माग गरेको छ । अध्यक्ष खत्रीले विशेष परिस्थितिमा सरकारकै निर्णय कार्यान्वयन गर्दा व्यवसायीमाथि कारबाही गरिएको आरोप लगाउँदै अब नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म श्रमिक नपठाउने स्पष्ट चेतावनी दिएका छन् ।

संघले आफ्ना सबै माग सम्बोधन नभएसम्म शून्य समय घोषणा गर्दै वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द रहने जनाएको छ । व्यवसायीहरूको यो निर्णयले वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा जान तयारी गरिरहेका हजारौं नेपाली श्रमिक प्रत्यक्ष प्रभावित हुने देखिएको छ ।

articles.title: सेती नदि थुनिएर ताल बन्यो, स्थानीय जाग्राम बस्न बाध्य
articles.summary:
कास्की । केहि दिन यताको निरन्तर वर्षाले पोखराको रामघाटमा सेती नदी थुनिएर विशाल ताल बनेको छ । जसका कारण नदिसँगै जोडिएका सुकुम्बासी बस्ती बाढीले बगाउने जोखिममा रहेका छन् ।

सेती नदीलाई लिएर पोखराको भौगोलिक बनावट अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेको चर्चा गरिन्छ , तर सेतिले निम्त्याएको जोखिम न्यून गर्न भने कुनै निकायको ध्यान पुग्न सकेको छैन । झट्ट हेर्दा यो दृश्य कुनै तालको होला भन्ने लाग्न सक्छ, तर नझुक्किनुस् यो कुनै ताल भने होइन ।

केहीदिन यता निरन्तर परेको वर्षको कारण सेती नदीमा पानीको बहाव निकै उच्च छ । हो पोखरा रामघाटमा फराकिलो रहेको सेती नदीको निकास सानो हुँदा पानी जान नसकेर विशाल ताल नै बनेको छ । सेती नदी थुनिएर ताल बन्दा अहिलेसम्म क्षति त भएको छैन तर संभावित क्षतिको जोखिम भने निकै बढेको छ ।

दाह संस्कारका लागि बनाइएका घाटहरु पुरै जलमग्न बनेका छन् । सेती किनारसँगै दुई दर्जन बढी सुकुम्बासी बस्ती छ, बर्खा लागे पछि कतिबेला बाढीले बगाउने हो भनेर जाग्राम बस्नु पर्ने अवस्था छ । अहिले ३ वर्ष यताकै ठूलो र डरलाग्दो तरिकाले सेती बढेको स्थानीय बताउँछन् ।

सेती नदी पोखराको अधिकांस भागमा भूमिगत भएर बगेको छ । पोखराको बीच भाग अर्थात् रामघाटमा भने सेती सतहमा देखिन्छ । यस आसपासको क्षेत्र अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेपनि सुकुम्बासीका नाममा बस्ती बस्ने क्रम भने नरोकिदो जोखिम झनै बढ्दैछ । पछिल्लो समय झनझन गहिरिदै गएको सेती खोंच र निरन्तरको बर्षाका कारण कतिबेला ठूलो दुर्घटना निम्तिने भन्ने इतिहासविद्को चिन्ता छ ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट र निरन्तर वर्षाले भासिन सक्ने सम्भाव्यताले पोखरालाई वर्षेनी जोखिम तर्फ धकेलेको भूगोलविद्को बुझाई छ । नदी थुनिएर आफ्नो गतिमा जान नपाउँदा निरन्तर जमिनलाई खियाउनाले जोखिम बढेको भूगोलविद् कृष्ण प्रसाद पौडेल बताउँछन् ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट, बेलाबेलामा भएका जमीन भासिने घटना र भूमिगतरूपमा बगेको सेतीका कारण पोखराको जोखिमबारे बेलाबेला चर्चा हुने गर्दछ, तर त्यो चर्चालाई दीर्घकालीन समाधानको बाटोतर्फ भने कुनै निकायले लैजान सकेका छैनन् ।

articles.title: स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धनमा जोड, दोलखामा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना
articles.summary:
दोलखा । जीवनको दिगो सुरुवातका लागि स्तनपान प्रभावकारी कार्यहरूको सुदृढीकरण“ भन्ने नारासहित दोलखाको भीमेश्वर नगरपालिका–५ स्थित माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीमा विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ मनाइएको छ । कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविकालाई प्रोत्साहन गरिएको छ ।

विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ को अवसरमा दोलखामा आयोजित कार्यक्रममा धुलिखेल अस्पताल दोलखाका विशेषज्ञ चिकित्सकहरूले गर्भवती महिलाको स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण, अल्ट्रासाउन्ड, स्वास्थ्य परामर्श तथा स्तनपान र शिशु पोषणबारे अभिमुखीकरण गरेका छन् ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमालाई पोषण सामग्री, ब्ल्यांकेट तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीका स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई छाता वितरण गरिएको छ । ती सामग्री पूर्व स्वास्थ्य चौकी प्रमुख रामकृष्ण मास्केको पहलमा विभिन्न दाताबाट संकलन गरिएको हो ।

कार्यक्रममा जिल्लाको स्वास्थ्य अवस्था, शिशु स्वास्थ्यमा आमाको दूधको महत्व र स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धन अभियानबारे जानकारी गराइएको छ । समुदायस्तरमा यस्ता कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिनुपर्नेमा जोड दिइएको छ ।

भीमेश्वर नगरपालिकाले मातृ तथा शिशु स्वास्थ्यलाई प्राथमिकतामा राख्दै स्वास्थ्य संस्थासँगको सहकार्यलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने जनाएको छ ।

नेपाल क्षयरोग निवारण संस्थाले समुदायमा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना अभिवृद्धिका कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिइने जनाएको छ ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई सम्मान गर्दै स्तनपानको महत्व समुदायसम्म पु¥याउने प्रयास गरिएको आयोजकले जनाएको छ ।

articles.title: भूपेन्द्रसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन शुरु
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं मूल्य बराबरको पूर्वाधार बिक्री प्रकरणले नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रमा ल्याएको तरंगको पराकम्प अझै कम भएको छैन । लाइसेन्स रद्द भएपछि राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने सम्पत्ति चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँमा बिक्री भएको विषय अहिले अनुसन्धानको केन्द्रमा छ ।

सीआईबीले पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन अघि बढाएको छ । नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्र एउटा प्रश्नले अझै तरंगित छ । राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं रुपैयाँ बराबरको सम्पत्ति कसरी निजी हातमा पुग्यो ? यसको जवाफ अझै मिल्न सकेको छैन । नेपाल प्रहरीको केन्द्रीय अनुसन्धान ब्युरो अर्थात् सीआईबीले यही प्रकरणमा नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणका पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीलाई पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान अघि बढाइरहेको छ ।

काठमाडौं जिल्ला अदालतले भण्डारीमाथि थप अनुसन्धानका लागि प्रहरीलाई ६ दिनको म्याद दिएको छ । उनीमाथि ठगी, आपराधिक विश्वासघात र संगठित अपराधसम्बन्धी कसुरमा अनुसन्धान भइरहेको छ ।

स्मार्ट टेलिकमले २०७० सालमा आधारभूत टेलिफोन सेवा सञ्चालनको अनुमति पाएको थियो । तर कम्पनीले नवीकरण दस्तुर र रोयल्टीबापतको करिब ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ सरकारलाई बुझाउन सकेन । त्यसपछि २०८० वैशाख ३ गते यसको लाइसेन्स स्वतः रद्द भयो ।

कानुनअनुसार लाइसेन्स रद्द भएको दूरसञ्चार कम्पनीको टावर, नेटवर्क, उपकरण र अन्य पूर्वाधार राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ । तर सीआईबीको आरोप छः राज्यको नाममा आइसकेको स्मार्ट टेलिकमको सम्पत्ति नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले गैरकानुनी रूपमा लिलामी ग¥यो र त्यो सम्पत्ति एनसेल आजियाटा लिमिटेडले खरिद ग¥यो । स्मार्टको लिलामी मूल्य थियो चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँ ।

सीआईबीका अनुसार यो प्रक्रियामा तत्कालीन दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीको भूमिका सबैभन्दा बढि शंकास्पद देखिएको छ । यही अनुसन्धानका क्रममा नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका अध्यक्ष पृथ्वीबहादुर पाण्डेसहित ६ जना सञ्चालकको बैंक खाता रोक्का गरिएको छ । प्रहरीले उनीहरूविरुद्ध पक्राउ पुर्जीसमेत लिएको बताइएको छ ।

खाता रोक्का भएका व्यक्तिमा अध्यक्ष पाण्डेसँगै प्रणय राजभण्डारी, दीपांकर शाक्य, कविकुमार तिव्रेवाला, शालिकराम बेलवासे र शोभा श्रेष्ठ रहेका छन् ।

अर्का सञ्चालक मदनकुमार आचार्यले भने सीआईबीमा उपस्थित भएर बयान दिइसकेका कारण पक्राउ पुर्जीबाट बाहिर रहेको बुझिएको छ ।

फेरि एकपटक बिक्रि प्रक्रियाको कुरा गरौँ

स्मार्ट टेलिकमकोे सम्पत्ति बिक्री प्रक्रिया नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले स्मार्ट टेलिकमले सम्पत्ति बिक्रिका लागि बोलपत्र आह्वान गरेसँगै अघि बढेको थियो । यसमा तीन कम्पनी सहभागी भए । ट्रान्सगेट टेकले ४४ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ, प्रोफेसनल बिजनेस नेटवर्कले ४२ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ र एनसेल आजियाटाले चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँको प्रस्ताव पेस ग¥यो ।

बैंकले सबैभन्दा बढी रकम प्रस्ताव गर्ने एनसेलको बोलपत्र स्वीकार ग¥यो । तर यी तीन कम्पनीले राखेको खरिद मूल्य प्रस्ताव नै शंकास्पद देखिन्छ । सेटिङमै तीन कम्पनी एकै व्यक्तिबाट परिचालित देखिन्छ । दुई कम्पनीको प्रस्तावभन्दा एनसेल आजियाटाको प्रस्ताव आकाश जमिन फरक छ ।

यो किनबेचमा बैंकको दाबी छ, उसले ऋण असुलीका लागि बैंक तथा वित्तीय संस्थासम्बन्धी ऐनको व्यवस्थाअनुसार धितो बिक्री गरेको हो । तर जुन सम्पत्ति राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आइसकेको थियो, त्यसलाई बैंकले बिक्री गर्ने अधिकार कसरी पायो भन्ने सीआईबीको प्रश्न छ ।

यसअघि सीआईबीले स्मार्ट टेलिकमका सञ्चालक सर्वेश जोशी र नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत ज्योति प्रकाश पाण्डेलाई पनि पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान गरेको थियो । सीआईबीले केही महिनादेखि यो प्रकरणमाथि अध्ययन अनुसन्धान गरिरहेको छ ।

तत्कालिन मन्त्री शर्माको भूमिका !

भूपेन्द्र भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि तत्कालिन सञ्चारमन्त्री रेखा शर्माका सल्लाहकार थिए । शर्माको जोडबलमा भण्डारीलाई प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्षमा तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री पुष्पकमल दाहाल ‘प्रचण्ड’ नेतृत्वको सरकारले नियुक्त गरेको थियो । प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि भण्डारी इन्टरग्रुप टेलिकम एसएल लिमिटेड र स्मार्ट मोबाइल बुरुन्डीको प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत भइसकेका व्यक्ति हुन् ।

उनले मरु डिजिटल वालेट चलाउने कम्पनी पेनेपमा अध्यक्षका रुपमा ५ वर्ष १० महिना काम गरेका थिए । कार्यकाल ७ महिना बाँकी छँदै प्राधिकरणका तत्कालीन अध्यक्ष पुरुषोत्तम खनालले तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री प्रचण्ड र तत्कालीन सञ्चारमन्त्री शर्माको दबाब खेप्न नसकेपछि २०८० पुस २४ गते राजीनामा दिएपछि भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रको नियामक प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष नियुक्त भएका थिए ।

वर्तमान सरकारले सार्वजनिक पदाधिकारीसम्बन्धी विशेष व्यवस्थाअन्तर्गत भण्डारीलाई पदबाट बर्खास्त गरेको हो । आलोचकहरूले भण्डारीको कार्यकालमा दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रका समस्या थप बढेको आरोप लगाएका छन् । स्मार्ट टेलिकमका टावर राख्न दिएका दुई सयभन्दा बढी घरधनीले समेत लामो समयदेखि भाडा नपाएको गुनासो गर्दै आएका छन् ।

सीआईबीको अनुसन्धानले राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनु पर्ने अर्बौ मूल्यको दूरसञ्चार पूर्वाधार कानूनी प्रक्रियाबाट बिक्रि भएको थियो कि मिलेमतोमा भन्ने प्रश्नको उत्तर खोजिरहेको छ । स्मार्ट टेलिकम प्रकरणको अन्तिम निष्कर्ष अनुसन्धान र अदालतको प्रक्रियाले तय गर्नेछ ।

articles.title: टुसा व्यापारमा कडाई, पोखरामा माग भन्दा कम आपूर्ति
articles.summary:
कास्की । साउन लागेसँगै पोखराको बजारमा पहाडी क्षेत्रमा पाइने औषधीय गुणयुक्त टुसाको कारोबार सुरु भएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने पर्यटकका लागि टुसा लोकप्रिय कोसेली बन्दै गए पनि यस वर्ष उत्पादन र आपूर्ति घट्दा व्यापार पनि सुस्त बनेको छ ।

अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजनाले चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरेसँगै बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको जनाएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने धेरैजसो आन्तरिक पर्यटक फर्किने बेला स्थानीय कोसेलीका रूपमा टुसा लैजान रुचाउँछन् ।

औषधीय गुणले भरिपूर्ण मानिने टुसाको तरकारी पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा झन् लोकप्रिय बन्दै गएको छ । अधिकांश टुसा पाइने क्षेत्र अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजना (एक्याप) अन्तर्गत पर्छन् । संरक्षणसँगै स्थानीयको आयआर्जनलाई समेत ध्यानमा राख्दै एक्यापले हरेक वर्ष साउन महिनाभर सर्वसाधारणलाई टुसा संकलन गर्न अनुमति दिने गरेको छ ।

असारदेखि भदौसम्म टुसा पलाउने मुख्य याम हो । कास्कीका ल्वाङ, घलेल, भुर्जुङखोला, सिक्लेस, ताङतिङ, याङजाकोट, घान्द्रुक, लान्द्रुक, धम्पुस र लुम्लेलगायत उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रबाट बजारमा टुसा ल्याइन्छ । मानव स्वास्थ्यका लागि उपयोगी भएकाले यसको महत्व हरेक वर्ष बढ्दै गएको एक्यापको भनाइ छ ।

साउन महिनामा धेरैले माछामासु कम खाने परम्परा र यही समयमा टुसाको उत्पादन बढी हुने भएकाले व्यापार पनि बढ्ने गरेको थियो । तर यस वर्ष भने बजारको अवस्था फरक देखिएको छ । व्यापारीका अनुसार उत्पादन कम भएकाले बजारमा टुसाको आपूर्ति घटेको छ ।

अहिले पोखरामा प्रतिमुठा ८० देखि १५० रुपैयाँसम्ममा बिक्री भइरहेको छ । राम्रो व्यापार भएका दिन एकै स्थानबाट दुई सय मुठासम्म बिक्री हुने गरे पनि अघिल्लो वर्षको तुलनामा यसपालि कारोबार घटेको व्यवसायीको भनाइ छ ।

पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा टुसाको चोरी निकासी बढेपछि एक्यापले व्यवस्थापन कडा बनाएको छ । बोलकबोल प्रक्रियामार्फत वैधानिक रूपमा संकलन र बिक्रीको व्यवस्था गरिएको छ ।

अघिल्ला वर्षमा करिब ९ लाख टुसा निकासा गरिएकोमा यस वर्ष ६ लाख मात्रै निकासा गरिएको र चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरिएकाले पनि बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको एक्यापले जनाएको छ ।

उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रको प्राकृतिक उत्पादन टुसा जडीबुटी मात्र होइन, पोखराको पहिचान बनेको कोसेली पनि हो । तर उत्पादनमा कमी र अवैध निकासी नियन्त्रणको प्रभाव यस वर्ष बजारमा स्पष्ट देखिएको छ ।

संरक्षण र व्यवस्थित व्यवस्थापनसँगै उत्पादन बढाउन सकिए टुसाको व्यापारले स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रलाई अझ बलियो बनाउने अपेक्षा समेत गरिएको छ ।

articles.title: महारथीको सम्मान लिन नेपाल आउँदै जनरल सेठ
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको पुरानो परम्परालाई निरन्तरता दिन भारतीय स्थल सेनाप्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ साउन ३१ गते नेपाल भ्रमणमा आउँदैछन् । मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान पाउने जनरल सेठको यो भ्रमणसँगै गोर्खा भर्ती, अग्निपथ योजना र सीमामा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि हुने व्यवहारका विषय पनि चर्चामा छन् ।

भारतीय स्थल सेनाका प्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ पाँच दिने औपचारिक भ्रमणका लागि साउन ३१ गते अर्थात् अगस्ट १६ मा नेपाल आउँदैछन् । नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देलको निमन्त्रणामा हुन लागेको यो भ्रमणलाई नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको निरन्तरताका रूपमा हेरिएको छ ।

भ्रमणका क्रममा जनरल सेठलाई नेपाली सेनाको मानार्थ महारथी दर्जाको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरिने कार्यक्रम छ । सन् १९५० देखि नेपाल र भारतले एकअर्काका सेना प्रमुखलाई मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान प्रदान गर्दै आएका छन् । यो परम्परालाई दुई देशबीचको विश्वास, मित्रता र सैनिक सहकार्यको एउटा विशिष्ट प्रतिक मानिएको छ ।

यसअघि २०८१ मंसिर २७ गते नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देललाई भारतको नयाँदिल्लीमा आयोजित विशेष समारोहमा भारतीय राष्ट्रपति द्रौपदी मुर्मुले भारतीय सेनाको मानार्थ महारथीको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरेकी थिइन् ।

नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्ध !

नेपाल र भारतबीचको सैनिक सम्बन्ध शताब्दीयौँ पुरानो मानिन्छ । स्वतन्त्र भारत र नेपालबीच सन् १९५० को शान्ति तथा मैत्री सन्धिपछि दुई देशबीचको रक्षा सहकार्य अझ संस्थागत बनेको हो । दुवै देशका सेनाले संयुक्त सैन्य अभ्यास सूर्य किरण, विपद् व्यवस्थापन, सीमा सुरक्षासम्बन्धी समन्वय, तालिम आदान–प्रदान तथा उच्च तहका भ्रमणलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै आएका छन् ।

यस्तै नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनामा भर्ती हुने व्यवस्था पनि दुई देशबीचको विशेष सम्बन्धको अर्को आधार हो ।

गोर्खा सैनिकका रूपमा नेपाली युवाले करिब दुई सय वर्षदेखि भारतीय सेनामा सेवा गर्दै आएका छन् । अहिले पनि हजारौँ नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनाका विभिन्न गोर्खा रेजिमेन्टमा कार्यरत छन् भने ठूलो संख्यामा पूर्वगोर्खा सैनिकले पेन्सन र अन्य सुविधा प्राप्त गरिरहेका छन् ।

अग्निपथले रोकिएको भर्ति !

तर पछिल्ला वर्षमा भारतीय सेनाको अग्निपथ योजना लागू भएपछि नेपाली नागरिकको भर्ती प्रक्रिया प्रभावित भएको छ । नेपाल सरकारले अग्निपथ योजनाबारे औपचारिक धारणा नटुंग्याएको भन्दै नेपाली युवाको भारतीय सेनामा नयाँ भर्ती रोकिएको अवस्था छ ।

चार वर्षे कार्यकाल र त्यसपछि २५ प्रतिशतलाई मात्रै नियमित सेवामा राखिने अग्गिपथ अन्तर्गतको मापदण्डका कारण लामो समयदेखि कायम रहेको गोर्खा भर्ती रोकिएको हो । यो विषयमा दुवै देशबीच कूटनीतिक तहमा छलफल हुँदै आएको छ ।

सीमा दुखेको सम्बन्ध !

नेपाली सेना र भारतीय सेनाबीच मानार्थ महारथीको विशिष्ट परम्परा रहँदा रहँदै पनि सीमामा भारतीय सीमा सुरक्षा बल एसएसबीले नेपाली नागरिकमाथि गर्ने दुव्र्यवहारका घटना बेलाबेला सार्वजनिक हुँदै आएका छन् ।

एसएसबीले सीमा क्षेत्रमा कुटपिट, अनावश्यक नियन्त्रण, गोली चलाइएका घटना तथा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि भएको दुव्र्यवहारले नेपाली नागरिकले अक्सर भारतसँग चित्त दुखाउनु परेको छ । यस्ता घटनापछि नेपाली पक्षबाट कूटनीतिक विरोध भएपनि दीर्घकालीन समाधान भने हुन सकेको छैन ।

articles.title: वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्डः एक्यान अध्यक्ष नेपाल
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल चार्टर्ड एकाउण्टेण्ट्स संघ (एक्यान) का अध्यक्ष अनुप नेपालले वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्ड भएको बताएका छन् ।

नेपाल अडिटर्स एसोसिएसन (अडान) को वार्षिक साधारण सभालाई सम्बोधन गर्दै उनले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा पारदर्शिता र वित्तीय सुशासन कायम गर्न लेखापरीक्षण क्षेत्रको भूमिका महत्वपूर्ण हुने बताए । उनले राज्यको राजस्व सङ्कलनलाई पारदर्शी बनाउन र व्यावसायिक क्षेत्रमा विश्वास अभिवृद्धि गर्न लेखापरीक्षकहरूले गरेको योगदानको प्रशंसा गरे ।

एक्यान र अडान दुवै संस्थाको साझा लक्ष्य नेपाली लेखा व्यवसायलाई थप मर्यादित, पारदर्शी र उत्तरदायी बनाउनु रहेको भन्दै उनले पेसागत हकहित र नीतिगत सुधारका लागि सहकार्य आवश्यक रहेको बताए ।

उनले आजको समय प्रविधिमैत्री युग रहेको भन्दै यसमा पनि अडिटर्सहरुले आफूलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउनुपर्नेमा जोड दिए । अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय लेखापरीक्षण मापदण्ड र कर प्रणालीका नयाँ चुनौतीहरूको सामना गर्नका दक्षता अभिवृद्धि गर्नुपर्ने उनको सुझाव छ । पछिल्लो समयको एआई प्रविधिहरुबाट कोही पनि आतंकित हुनु नपर्ने भन्दै प्रविधिलाई केवल एउटा साधनका रूपमा लिन उनले आग्रह गरे ।

उनले क्याल्कुलेटरको आविष्कारको उदाहरण दिँदै क्याकुलेटर आज सामान्य र आवश्यक भएजस्तै एआई जस्ता प्रविधिहरु आगामी दशकमा उस्तै अत्यावश्यक बन्ने बताए ।

खासगरी उच्च व्यावसायिक नैतिकता, निष्पक्षता र इमानदारितालाई आत्मसाथ गरि समाज र राज्यको लेखापरीक्षण पेशाप्रतिको विश्वासलाई मजबुत बनाउनुपर्नेमा उनले जोड दिएका छन् ।

articles.title: Fresh royal massacre probe hits roadblock before it begins
articles.summary:
The government’s announcement to reopen the investigation into Nepal’s 25-year-old royal massacre has failed to move forward as authorities remain undecided on how the inquiry should be conducted.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung announced a fresh investigation immediately after taking office for the second time. But the government has yet to decide whether Nepal Police should handle the probe or a separate commission should be formed.

The uncertainty over the investigation model has stalled the process.

A day after assuming office on June 9, Gurung held discussions with Nepal Police Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki, security chiefs and senior officials at the Ministry of Home Affairs. During the meeting, Gurung instructed officials to explore ways to investigate the massacre through Nepal Police.

However, police officials advised that a Cabinet-level decision would be more appropriate because the massacre had already been investigated by a commission led by then chief justice Keshav Prasad Upadhyaya, with then speaker Taranath Ranabhat and opposition leader Madhav Kumar Nepal as members.

“Since a judicial inquiry commission had already investigated the incident and submitted a report, the police view was that simply forming another committee would not necessarily lead to a conclusion,” a senior home ministry official said. “A decision has still not been made on whether to assign the investigation to police or set up a separate commission.”

Home Minister Gurung, however, refused to disclose details about the progress of the probe. In a recent interview with Kantipur he said, “Home Ministry cannot disclose sensitive information,” he said.

“The Home Ministry is not really a place for providing sensitive information; some things can only be discussed at the surface level,” he said.

Officials from specialised crime investigation units, including the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) and Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, also said no investigation had begun so far.

According to senior officials at the ministry, police leadership had already briefed the home minister about three major obstacles in reopening the case.

“During the meeting with security chiefs after the minister’s decision, police officials explained that the absence of crime scene records and postmortem reports would create difficulties,” a ministry official said. “Another challenge is that there was no ballistic examination to determine what weapons were used.”

Investigators who spoke to Kantipur also said a fresh probe would face major scientific challenges because crucial evidence, including the type of weapons and bullets used, the nature of injuries and whether wounds were consistent with the official account, was not available.

“Police investigations are conducted with the purpose of prosecution. What matters is whether facts and evidence can support a case in court,” an official familiar with the police briefing said. “Based on the evidence currently available, it appears difficult to reach any conclusion. That makes a police-led investigation complicated.”

Nepal Police former superintendent Sher Bahadur Karki, who was assigned to photograph the crime scene after the June 2001 massacre, said even documenting the scene had been delayed.

He recalled reaching the site only five days after the incident and said conducting an investigation now would be extremely difficult.

“I don’t think photographs alone will provide much assistance today. Many things would have to be based on assumptions,” Karki told Kantipur. “However, some eyewitnesses are still alive, and their statements could reveal new information.”

Karki said that if the original structure of the palace had remained unchanged, investigators might have been able to understand the scene more easily through photographs, but major changes over the years would make the process harder.

A senior police official familiar with discussions between police and the home minister said the original report was the only substantial basis currently available for a new investigation.

“The key question is whether the people who prepared that report reached their conclusions objectively or under pressure or influence,” the official said. “If they provide new facts, that could change things. Otherwise, there does not appear to be much basis for taking the investigation much further.”

On June 4, 2001, then king, Gyanendra, formed a three-member panel to investigate the massacre. However, then opposition leader Madhav Kumar Nepal resigned from the panel.

“We were at the Birendra Military Hospital in Chhauni when the decision to form the committee was announced,” recalled Deviram Sharma, who was then chief of the National Investigation Department.

“Initially, opposition leader Nepal himself had asked to be included in the committee. Later, for reasons unknown, he decided to withdraw.”

After Nepal’s withdrawal, the two-member panel submitted a report suggesting that Crown Prince Dipendra had carried out the massacre by opening fire on members of the royal family.

Statements from most members of the royal family who were present at the palace that night also claimed that Dipendra was responsible for the shooting.

According to the report, a total of at least 24 members of the royal family and relatives had gathered for a dinner at the Tribhuvan Sadan building inside Narayanhiti Royal Palace on June 1, 2001.

The report said Dipendra spent some time alone playing billiards in the billiards room at around 7:30pm. It also cited statements that he had consumed whisky neat before joining the gathering

“Before King Birendra arrived at the hall, it appeared that Dipendra was unable to control his body, and Prince Nirajan, Prince Paras, Kumar Gorakh Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana [the king’s son-in-law], and Dr Rajiv Shah had taken Dipendra to his private quarters,” the report stated.

The report said that while Dipendra was in his room, he called his aide Gajendra Bohara at 8:19pm and ordered him to bring cigarettes. According to the inquiry, royal attendant Ram Krishna KC prepared a special cigarette containing cannabis and another unidentified black substance and handed it to Paras through the eastern door of the billiards room.

The investigation also examined telephone records obtained from then Nepal Telecommunications Corporation. The records showed that Dipendra had three conversations with Devyani Rana before the shooting.

Rana, who was receiving treatment in India at the time, told investigators that she noticed Dipendra’s speech was slurred and asked his aides Gajendra Bohara and Raju Karki to check on him.

According to attendant Ram Krishna KC’s statement cited in the report, Dipendra changed into camouflage fatigues after speaking with Rana and came out of his private quarters carrying weapons.

When an attendant offered to bring his emergency bag, Dipendra reportedly replied that it was not needed at the time.

The report said Dipendra then entered the billiards room carrying a rifle and a 12-bore shotgun.

According to the commission’s account, Dipendra first fired at the ceiling and western wall of the room with a black-coloured gun. He then opened fire on his father, King Birendra, who was talking with other guests, before moving outside and throwing the weapon near bushes beside the inner garden.

The report stated that Dipendra then returned to the billiards room carrying a rifle equipped with a light and telescope and opened fire again.

The inquiry report described a series of shootings that killed or injured members of the royal family, including King Birendra, Queen Aishwarya, Prince Nirajan, Princess Shruti, Princess Shanti, Princess Sharada, Princess Jayanti Shah, Dhirendra Shah (the king’s brother who no longer held the title of prince), Kumar Khadga Bikram Shah (king’s brother-in-law), and others.

The commission said its account was based on statements from people present at the scene, including Princess Shobha, then prince Paras, Kumar Gorakh Shamsher, Ketaki Chester, Rabi Shumsher, Dr Rajiv Shah and Maheshwar Kumar Singh.

Despite the official inquiry’s conclusion, public speculation and conspiracy theories surrounding the incident have continued for more than two decades, prompting periodic calls for a fresh investigation.

articles.title: Nepal’s para table tennis players train on borrowed gear but dream of Asian Games medals
articles.summary:
Every evening, a hall just inside the main gate of the Nepal Disabled Association’s Khagendra New Life Home in Jorpati, Kathmandu, hums with activity. Except on Saturdays, when the routine shifts to the morning, the space is filled with the rhythmic percussion of training—the sharp click of balls meeting rackets, their quick pop against the tables, and the clatter across the concrete floor whenever a shot is missed.

In the rare moments of silence, the rhythm of play gives way to quiet replenishment: athletes catching their breath or meticulously applying fresh rubber to their rackets with practiced hands.

They are expensive, echoed five para table tennis players training for the 5th Asian Para Games as they glued the rubber on Thursday. These are second-hand rubbers they brought from Japan by requesting the players there. They cannot afford new ones themselves.

In Nepal, a basic set of two rackets and three balls can be purchased for less than Rs500. But neither these budget options nor professional gear costing thousands more are standardised for the specific requirements of international competition.

“I recall being denied a racket that cost me thousands of rupees during a Paralympic qualification event,” said Keshav Thapa, who is currently preparing for his third Asian Para Games. A wheelchair user, Thapa has previously represented Nepal at the 2018 and 2022 Asian Para Games in Indonesia and China. “I ended up competing using a borrowed racket from another participant,” Thapa said.

Should athletes be paying out of pocket to represent their country at major international events like the Asian Para Games? While global sports standards demand robust state sponsorship, for Nepal’s para table tennis players, self-funding is a grim, routine reality. This systemic government neglect forces athletes to rely on second-hand rubbers sourced from Japan and borrowed rackets just to remain competitive. Despite their proven potential—exemplified by continental medals and unwavering dedication—these players must navigate a precarious landscape where empty pockets and state indifference stand in stark contrast to their resolve to bring home glory.

Nepal has participated in the Asian Para Games since its inaugural edition in Gwangzhou, China, in 2010. But the country sent athletes for table tennis at the Games only from the second edition in South Korea in 2014. Hira Niraula and Ram Prasad Kharel represented Nepal in table tennis then.

At the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Indonesia, four table tennis players—Thapa, Sonika Dhakal, Lek Bahadur KC and Raikosha Shahi—represented Nepal.

KC has not played of late, while Shahi is currently the treasurer at the National Physical Disabled Table Tennis Association (NPDTTA). Shahi reaches the hall in Jorpati to manage the boards and other equipment before any players arrive for training. Thapa and Dhakal, meanwhile, are still competing.

On Thursday, Dhakal was the first to arrive at the training hall. She greeted Shahi as soon as she saw her, pushing the rims of her wheelchair. Dhakal had travelled a long way to get here, from Sanga in Bhaktapur, over 20 kilometres away, where she works as a peer counsellor at the Spinal Injury Rehabilitation Centre. “The bus picks me up at 6:55am and drops me off at around 5pm, the time when my training commences,” she said, as she entered the hall and started stretching her arms with the second-hand rubber bands brought from Japan.

Dhakal, who is 42, is training for her fourth participation at the Asian Para Games. She was one of the first Nepali athletes to participate at the Asian Para Games in China in 2010. But Dhakal was then a para swimmer.

“I found swimming expensive,” Dhakal said with a laugh. She was in for a rude shock when she found out table tennis was not a cheap sport either, she said.

After shifting to table tennis, Dhakal has represented Nepal in the sport at the Asian Para Games in South Korea and Indonesia. “I did not participate in the previous edition in China in 2023 as I could not afford it,” Dhakal lamented.

Alongside Thapa and Dhakal, five other para table tennis players are aiming to represent Nepal in Japan. All of them have played for the country at international tournaments in the past—out of their pockets.

“We have made up our minds to spend the required amount ourselves this time as well,” said Digam Sing Chemjong, one among the seven para table tennis players aiming to represent Nepal in Japan.

Chemjong was one of the two para swimmers, alongside Dhakal, from Nepal at the 2010 Asian Para Games. He then also led the national wheelchair cricket team as its captain. It was during his captainship that Nepal won their first tri-series in 2017 by defeating India and Bangladesh at the TU Ground.

“In the end, I found solace in table tennis,” Chemjong said. “My biggest reason to take up sports is to win medals and trophies for the country. Though the state has neglected us, we have not stopped loving our country.”

The government has allocated Rs3.5 million for the country’s participation at the Asian Para Games in Japan. There are expected to be at least three dozen athletes across around a dozen sports from Nepal. And the budget allocated does not even cover a one-way fare for these athletes, let alone coaches and officials required to support these athletes with disabilities.

Chemjong, who also visits the National Table Tennis Training Centre in Lainchaur during the mornings, said he had to wait for three days in his wheelchair—with a bat in his hands—to be called to play by able-bodied athletes.

“Can you even play table tennis in a wheelchair? Can you play these strokes? These are the questions I faced at the beginning in Lainchaur around three months ago,” Chemjong said. “But once I got a chance to play, many were shocked. Now, they call me to play with them.”

Chemjong said that there is not much difference between table tennis players on a wheelchair and those who are physically able. “All you need is the hunger to give your best,” he added.

Alongside Thapa, Dhakal and Chemjong, Lali Tamang and Bibek Rai are also aiming for another shot at a table tennis medal at the Asian Para Games.

Rai, who works at Dharan Sub-metropolitan City and trains locally, had participated in Hangzhou, China, in 2023. Tamang, who currently works at the Vocational Opportunity for Inclusion to Community and Employment (VOICE) project run by Spinal Injury Sangh Nepal (SISN), represented Nepal in the previous Asian Para Games as well.

While the 2023 event was Rai’s first participation at the Asian main event, Tamang was a wheelchair runner at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Indonesia.

“I left athletics after I got to see the difference between foreign para athletes and us in Indonesia,” Tamang said. “They had quality wheelchairs. When I asked how much it cost, the answer was over Rs1 million. Then, I decided to shift to table tennis believing it would be cheaper and better.”

But the lack of support from the state has made table tennis an expensive game, too.

“I want to win medals for the country and motivate many others like us to come outside and challenge the world,” Tamang said. “I do not care if I have to invest in it myself.”

And it is the same reason why emerging table tennis players have also decided to continue the sport.

For Nirmala Bhandari, 23, for instance, it has not been long since she started playing table tennis. After just a couple of months of training, she represented Nepal at the 2025 Asian Youth Para Games in Dubai.

After she arrived at the training hall in Jorpati on Thursday evening, riding her scooter for around an hour from Lalitpur, Bhandari said that she was highly motivated after seeing many athletes like her leaving their mark at the Asian Youth Para Games.

“When I asked those foreign athletes about the support they received back home, I felt jealous,” Bhandari said. “From receiving training at the places that were near and accessible to being provided with other necessary equipment, they have all the support. Back in our country, even finding an accessible training area is a herculean task.”

However, Bhandari, who spent handsomely while travelling to Dubai, does not want to quit anytime soon.

“I will continue playing table tennis until I can,” said Bhandari, who is currently pursuing her Master’s degree in Journalism. “I do not care if I have to spend all the hard-earned money on this sport and try winning medals for the country.”

So are these athletes ready to take on the world? The response from their volunteer coach Basanta Bharati is an emphatic yes.

“I am fully confident that these players can challenge the best in the world,” Bharati told the Post. “They might not win, but they are not easy to beat… The fire in them burns very bright. But they need more support from the state.”

Bharati adds he is quite optimistic about his players winning medals in Japan.

“These players are training very hard,” Bharati said as he showed hand-weight bands that weighed from half a kilo to a kilogram that were worn by the players to improve their strokes. “For instance, let’s see Swikrit Neupane. He already won a silver medal at the Asian Youth Para Games in Dubai last year.”

Neupane is currently training in his hometown of Biratnagar. “I have my examinations underway and could not be in Kathmandu for training,” Neupane, who is pursuing a Bachelor in Computer Application, told the Post over a phone call.

Rai and Neupane are two players who do not play in a wheelchair. They both fall in Class 7.

Wheelchair table tennis players fall under Classes 1-5 while those with physical impairment and who play while standing fall under Classes 6-10. There is also Class 11 for athletes with an intellectual impairment.

Neupane, who ranks 357th in the world among standing men’s singles, has been playing table tennis for over a decade. He dedicates his table tennis journey to coach Biken Thapa, who operates Stellar Table Tennis Training Centre in Biratnagar. “After my family’s support, it was coach Biken who trusted in me,” he said.

Even Chemjong has praised Thapa’s training centre as one of the best in Eastern Nepal. “I have trained and played there many times,” Chemjong said. “The most beautiful thing is that the centre is wheelchair-friendly. And coach Biken is very experienced.”

Neupane, 22, sees a good future in table tennis. “My family was very happy when I won silver last year, though I had to spend a good amount of money for travel and accommodation, among others,” he said. “I even got honoured by the provincial and local authorities. The whole community praised me. It was a great moment.”

Neupane’s medal-winning journey further exposes the state's systemic neglect of para athletes. While the Sports Development Guidelines, 2079, reserve cash incentives exclusively for Paralympic medalists, the government offers no such recognition for success in the Asian Youth Para Games or Asian Para Games. Yet, despite years of official indifference, the para table tennis squad remains driven by a singular, defiant purpose: to bring home medals for Nepal.

Thapa, the athlete, however, lamented that they do not even have a proper wheelchair. “We use the ones that are available and have come through someone’s support,” he said. “We need a sports wheelchair, which is extremely expensive.”

Citing Palesha Goverdhan’s historic medal in Paris 2024, Thapa said he believes para athletes will soon get the state’s attention again. “It shall start from the Asian Para Games in Japan,” he said. “We will give our best to win medals for the country.”

articles.title: Nepal is growing more rice but losing indigenous varieties
articles.summary:
Until a decade ago, the paddies of Nepal’s Tarai were dominated by rice varieties whose names were deeply woven into the region’s farming culture: Sona Mansuli, Soni, Katarni, Savitri, Ram Dhan, Radha-4, Sawadhan and Swarna, also known as Ardinath.

By this time of year, the fields would already be green with these familiar varieties, their cultivation tied to generations of farming knowledge and the agricultural rhythms of the plains.

These were more than traditional crops. They were adapted to the Tarai’s soil and climate and had long formed the backbone of farming communities in what is considered Nepal’s food basket.

Today, many of these varieties are disappearing.

Across the Tarai, and particularly in Madhesh province, farmers are steadily replacing indigenous rice with imported hybrid varieties. Some traditional varieties have become so rare that they are now at risk of disappearing altogether. Others survive only because a handful of farmers continue to grow them, sometimes despite government restrictions.

The shift is largely driven by economics.

Traditional rice varieties generally take longer to mature, produce lower yields and are increasingly vulnerable to disease. Hybrid varieties, by contrast, promise farmers higher yields in a shorter period, allowing them to harvest rice earlier and prepare their fields for another crop.

“The disappearance of traditional rice varieties is unfortunate,” said Surendra Prasad Kurmi, chief of the Agriculture Knowledge Centre in Rautahat district in south-central Nepal. “Disease outbreaks around harvest time have also been a major reason. Farmers have been abandoning these varieties for about a decade.”

Sabitri, Ram Dhan and Radha-4 can take 140 to 160 days to mature and typically produce three to four tonnes per hectare. Hybrid varieties mature in 120 to 130 days and can produce six to eight tonnes.

For farmers working on increasingly tight margins, the difference is difficult to ignore.

In Rautahat, farmers now grow hybrid varieties such as Gorkhanath and Loknath, whose seeds are imported from India or China. Their popularity reflects a broader transformation in the Tarai’s rice fields, where the pressure to produce more food in less time is steadily reshaping what farmers plant.

Even Sona Mansuli, once among the country’s most popular varieties, has become a complicated part of this transition.

The government banned its cultivation five years ago after repeated outbreaks of blast disease. Yet the variety remains popular with farmers, who continue to plant it despite the restriction.

“Farmers are still secretly growing Sona Mansuli,” Kurmi said.

Seeds of Soni, Katarni and Ram Dhan are also being brought in from India.

Nepal has 69 documented indigenous rice varieties, Kurmi said. But most are now struggling to survive.

“Most of them are on the verge of disappearing,” he said. “Only about 5 percent are still being cultivated.”

Among the varieties whose cultivation has declined are Baspate, Kankajira, Ratuwa, Sugandha, Pahadi Anadi, Madheshi Masino, Eklo Pahele, Sawa, Ram Dhan, Sabitri, Radha-4, Sawadhan, Ardinath-1 and Sukha-2 and Sukha-4.

The decline of these varieties is not simply a story of farmers choosing one seed over another. It reflects a much broader change in the way agriculture is being practised in the Tarai, as farmers respond to rising costs, changing weather and the need to make the most of increasingly limited land and time.

Changing weather patterns are making traditional farming harder. Erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells and the spread of new diseases are adding to the risks.

Agricultural experts say traditional varieties are also losing their natural resistance to diseases such as blast, sheath blight and bacterial leaf blight. At the same time, the cost of fertiliser, ploughing, labour and irrigation continues to rise, leaving farmers with little room to experiment with varieties that may offer lower returns.

For farmers such as Rudhal Chaudhary of Simra Bhawanipur, the calculation is straightforward.

“Until 10 years ago, farmers would go out of their way to plant Sona Mansuli,” he said. “Even though the government has banned it, farmers still prefer it.”

The timing of the harvest matters almost as much as the yield.

A rice variety that matures early gives farmers time to plant mustard, lentils or wheat during the winter season. Traditional varieties can take weeks longer to mature, making it harder to fit a second crop into the agricultural calendar.

For farmers trying to maximise the use of their land throughout the year, that delay can translate directly into lost income.

It has further reduced the appeal of traditional varieties.

But the disappearance of indigenous rice carries costs that may not be immediately visible in a farmer’s field.

As farmers switch to higher-yielding varieties, Nepal is also losing genetic diversity built up over generations. Indigenous varieties developed through years of cultivation were often naturally suited to particular soils, weather conditions and local farming practices.

Radha-4, for example, can tolerate dry conditions, while other local varieties are better adapted to flooding. Such characteristics may become increasingly important as Nepal’s climate becomes more unpredictable.

Once a variety disappears from farmers’ fields, the genetic traits it carries can also be lost permanently.

That is what worries farmers and agricultural experts who see the transition not simply as a change in farming preferences but as a potential threat to agricultural biodiversity and, ultimately, food security.

Jagendra Sahani, an old farmer in the district, worries that commercialisation could come at a high cost.

“It is natural for agriculture in Madhesh to become more commercial, but the complete disappearance of traditional varieties is a serious concern for food security and agricultural biodiversity,” he said. “Unless farmers are encouraged and supported to preserve indigenous seeds, varieties such as Sabitri, Ram Dhan and Radha-4 could soon exist only in agricultural textbooks and history.”

The dilemma facing farmers is therefore not simply whether to grow traditional rice or hybrids. Farmers need varieties that can provide sufficient yields, withstand disease and changing weather, mature within a workable agricultural calendar and generate enough income to sustain their households.

For many, hybrid varieties currently offer the most practical answer.

About 98 percent of the district’s rice planting has been completed this year. Rice covers around 34,000 hectares in Rautahat, according to the Agriculture Knowledge Centre.

Much of that land is now being planted with varieties that promise farmers more rice in less time.

The slow disappearance of Kalanamak

The story is particularly striking in Kapilvastu, where another traditional variety is fading from the landscape.

Kalanamak rice is soft and flavourful, with a distinctive fragrance. Until two decades ago, it was a familiar presence in local kitchens and was often served to guests as a mark of hospitality.

Today, fields of Kalanamak are increasingly difficult to find.

The variety was once a source of pride and a defining part of Kapilvastu’s agricultural identity. It was grown across parts of Kapilvastu, Rupandehi and southern parts of West Nawalparasi.

But Kalanamak is demanding.

It takes longer to mature than most other varieties, needs more water and requires greater care. It is also vulnerable to disease, pests and other crop stresses. The cost of growing it has risen while the returns have remained comparatively low.

“It is delicious, but expensive to produce and takes longer to mature,” said Rakesh Ojha, chief of the programme implementation unit of the National Agriculture Modernisation Programme. “That is why farmers choose improved varieties.”

The decline has been dramatic.

About 15 years ago, Kalanamak was grown on 4,000 to 5,000 hectares in Kapilvastu. Today, cultivation has fallen to barely 75 hectares, according to Ghanashyam Chaudhary, chief of the district’s Agriculture Knowledge Centre.

The change can be seen in the fields themselves. The dark Kalanamak panicles that once appeared across the landscape have become rare, replaced by the yellow-gold heads of newer varieties.

For Khursed Ahmed Khan, an agricultural expert, the disappearance of Kalanamak is not simply a loss for farmers. It is also the erosion of a part of Kapilvastu’s heritage, he says, yet local and provincial authorities have done little to preserve it.

“It is a grain with a history going back centuries,” he said. “But no one seems interested in protecting it.”

The rice is also distinctive in appearance. Farmers say its dark colour is what gave it the name Kalanamak, literally referring to its dark appearance.

Its history, however, reaches much further back.

Bhikkhu Siri Vajira, an assistant professor at Lumbini Buddhist University, claims Kalanamak has links to the Buddha era.

According to the tradition he recounts, about 2,600 years ago, when Gautam Buddha was preparing to leave Baishali, local people asked him for a keepsake. Buddha had little with him except his alms bowl.

“He took a handful of rice from his alms bowl and gave it to them,” Vajira said. “He told them to plant it in a marshy area. He said it would become fragrant and asked them to remember him when they smelled its aroma.”

During the Buddha era, a rice festival was held on the full moon of the Nepali month of Ashadh (June-July) outside the royal palace at Tilaurakot. Kalanamak was planted there, and rice made from the harvest was served in the royal palace, according to Vajira.

“This rice is very old,” he said. “But it has gradually disappeared.”

For those who see the rice as part of the cultural heritage of the Lumbini region, its decline also represents a missed economic opportunity.

Lilamani Sharma, president of the Lumbini Hotel Association, says Kalanamak’s historical association with the Buddhist era could be turned into an economic opportunity by developing it as a distinctive brand.

He believes the rice could be grown around Lumbini and marketed under the “Saras” brand, named after the sarus crane, another species associated with the region’s Buddhist heritage. Hotels in Lumbini and Kapilvastu could then serve Kalanamak rice to tourists as part of a campaign to preserve the traditional crop while creating a market for it.

Kalanamak is widely regarded as an organically grown rice variety, and Sharma says it could be promoted as rice dating back to the time of Buddha.

The rice also has an unusual connection with the sarus crane, one of the world’s rarest cranes. Farmers say the birds favour Kalanamak fields and often build their nests among the rice plants. Linking the rice with the crane could therefore give the variety a distinctive identity, Sharma said. The sarus crane itself is also associated with stories and traditions from the Buddhist era.

Barmeli and Jarneli also disappearing

The decline of traditional rice is not confined to the Tarai. Indigenous varieties have also been disappearing from Nepal’s hill districts, including Palpa.

Until about two decades ago, farmers in the hills commonly grew indigenous varieties. Today, seeds of some of those varieties survive only in a handful of places.

Farmers say they abandoned them because they produce less, are more labour-intensive, require plenty of water and take longer to mature.

Gopal Kafle of Lamdikhola in ward 9 of Rampur Municipality still remembers growing traditional rice. He says finding seeds of many of the varieties once grown in the area has now become increasingly difficult.

“Varieties such as Chhote, Barmeli, Anadi, Jarneli, Batisaro, Thapachini, Basmati, Kalo Jhinuwa, Jhinuwa and Aamjhotte, which were traditionally planted here, are now very difficult to find,” he said, recalling the old varieties. “The importance of traditional rice is disappearing in the villages. There are hardly any farmers left who grow them. More people are planting seeds bought from the market.”

Some members of the younger generation have never even heard of the varieties, Kafle said. The problem is no longer simply that farmers have stopped growing them. Their seeds are disappearing as well.

Once farmers stop maintaining a traditional variety, its seed can become increasingly difficult to obtain. Over time, the variety may disappear not only from the fields but also from the local knowledge and seed networks that sustained it.

Some varieties are already considered endangered, said Krishna Prasad Aryal, a farmer from ward 6 of Rampur Municipality.

Farmers have increasingly turned to commercially available seeds because they produce higher yields and require less water, he said.

“People want rice that can produce more from a smaller area, which is one reason the old varieties are becoming so difficult to find,” Aryal said. “In many cases, the seeds themselves are beginning to disappear. You might still find them in remote villages, but elsewhere they are very hard to come by.”

The transition is also being accelerated by changes in rural labour and farming technology.

Farmers have moved away from traditional rice because newer varieties produce more grain, have shorter stalks and are easier to manage, said Narayan Prasad Gaire, head of the agriculture section at Rampur Municipality.

Hybrid and improved varieties produce significantly higher yields than traditional rice. Modern machinery has also made harvesting and threshing easier, while the migration of young people from villages to work abroad has reduced the availability of farm labour.

“People may also be moving away from traditional varieties because they want more production with less effort,” Gaire said. “Traditional rice tends to be tastier and more filling, but the younger generation is no longer paying much attention to it.”

Some farmers now grow traditional varieties only for festivals and special occasions, he said.

Although rice from the old varieties is considered tastier, their lower yields, higher water requirements, long stalks and tendency to fall over before ripening have pushed farmers towards hybrid varieties.

According to the Directorate of Agriculture Development under the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, 7,287 hectares of land in the district is suitable for rice cultivation.

articles.title: What Nepali cinema has changed—and what it hasn’t
articles.summary:
Before the lights dimmed, the audience was already split between two worlds. Some had come to revisit a past they once lived through. Others had only heard stories about it.

The Film Development Board’s ‘Old Is Gold’ offers more than a chance to revisit old Nepali films. The exhibition features ten digitised films, including ‘Aama’, ‘Sindoor’, ‘Pariwartan’, ‘Manko Baandh’, ‘Kumari’, ‘Jeevan Rekha’, ‘Badlindo Aakash’, ‘Ke Ghar Ke Dera’, ‘Shantideep and Hijo Aaja Bholi’.

According to Film Development Board chairperson Dinesh DC, the programme was conceived as more than an anniversary event.

“An anniversary should not only mean cutting a cake and exchanging greetings,” he says. “A good way for an institution to mark its anniversary is also by bringing the history it has preserved back before the public.”

The technical development of Nepali cinema is immediately visible. Camera quality, sound, editing and production have improved significantly over the decades.

In ‘Sindoor’ conversations often unfold through long, largely static shots, while transitions between scenes can feel abrupt to viewers accustomed to the quicker cuts and multiple camera angles of contemporary cinema.

The films preserve not only stories but fragments of everyday life: of streets that no longer exist, fashions long abandoned, accents that have softened with time, and homes built around values that have since evolved.

Songs appear frequently, sometimes interrupting the narrative in ways that can feel excessive today, yet they generated some of the strongest audience reactions. Viewers clapped along when familiar songs began. Among them was Sumit, 37, who had brought his children, aged eight and thirteen, to introduce them to older Nepali cinema. The children said the songs were what they enjoyed most.

DC says that was one of the aims of the exhibition.

“I don’t want to call young people into the hall to give them a history lesson,” he says. “I want them to come, watch the films, enjoy them and start asking themselves questions about what Nepal was like at the time.”

Fashion is one obvious marker of change. Women frequently appear in saris and more traditional attire, contrasting with the broader urban and global influences visible in contemporary Nepali films.

Some romantic conventions now appear exaggerated. During ‘Sindoor’, the audience laughed at prolonged exchanges of glances between the romantic leads that were played seriously in the film.

Yet what now feels clichéd was still being established at the time; films like these helped define conventions later Nepali cinema repeatedly returned to.

At the same time, not everything feels distant. One of the more striking continuities is the way women are represented.

In ‘Aama’, for instance, Harka repeatedly abuses his wife, yet she is still expected to remain within the marriage and endure his behaviour. The scene reflects the limited choices available to women within the social world the film depicts.

Filmmaker and film educator Abhimanyu Dixit says the social shift is more complicated. Older films often relied on archetypes like the dutiful wife, sacrificial mother or “bad woman”, though he notes that some characters still had considerable agency. “Sometimes I watch and think, ‘did we actually become more conservative later?’” he says.

Dixit does not entirely agree that contemporary cinema simply reproduces the same stereotypes in more polished forms. “I actually think contemporary Nepali filmmakers are trying,” he says. “Even compared to 2018, when I used to review Nepali cinema for the Post, I can see a change.”

“You can watch a filmmaker’s work over several films, sometimes even within the same series, and see that their female characters have continued to evolve,” he says. Dixit attributes that partly to the current cultural climate and greater scrutiny from audiences. “Maybe social media scares filmmakers now, so they are more conscious. Or maybe we are genuinely learning.”

DC himself describes old cinema as a “visual document” of its period.

“When we watch an old film, we do not only watch a story,” he says. “We see the cities and villages of that time, the houses, clothes, language, family structures and the way society looked at men and women.”

For older viewers, the films also operate differently.

Sixty-seven-year-old Yogesh Parajuli said watching ‘Aama’ reminded him of a period when going to the cinema itself felt different.

“We used to bunk classes whenever there was a show,” he said. “Our mother used to come and chase us out. This made me miss her.”

That contrast between old and new audiences became one of the more interesting parts of the exhibition. Older viewers often recognised songs, actors and scenes immediately. Younger viewers responded to the films with more distance, sometimes laughing at the acting or dialogue, but still remaining engaged.

For the Board, this is also part of a larger archival project.

DC distinguishes between digitisation, restoration and preservation, noting that the three are not the same. The ten films in the exhibition have been digitised and made suitable for screening, while the Board is also preparing to digitise additional historically significant films.

He argues, however, that preserving only a limited number of films is not enough.

“Ten films are something to be proud of, but we cannot be satisfied with ten,” he says. “This is a beginning, not a destination.”The challenge extends beyond digitisation. Old reels, negatives, scripts, photographs and other material remain scattered across private collections, while copyright and ownership can limit how digitised films are publicly distributed.

Screenings including ‘Aama’, ‘Sindoor’ and ‘Pariwartan’ drew strong attendance, with some shows filling the hall.

For viewers, the exhibition offers a direct comparison between different periods of Nepali cinema. The cameras are sharper, editing is faster, fashion and romance have changed, and filmmakers are reconsidering how women are represented. Yet songs still draw audiences in, familiar storytelling conventions persist, and some older social attitudes remain recognisable.

‘Old Is Gold’ is therefore most interesting not simply as an exercise in nostalgia, but as a record of what Nepali cinema has changed, what it has retained and what it is still learning to leave behind.

articles.title: Gas shortages require swift government response
articles.summary:
The Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) market in Nepal currently faces a paradox where consumers experience shortages despite government officials claiming that imports from India remain steady. This recurring crisis has resurfaced less than two weeks after the Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) restored the sale of full-sized, 14.2 kg cylinders. The statistics maintained by the NOC tell an interesting story. During the initial stages of the West Asian conflict in February-March, the corporation supplied 51,192 tonnes of gas. LPG supply has remained steady, hovering around 40,000 tonnes per month till June-July. This trend indicates that the volume of fuel entering the country is not the primary driver of the current scarcity.

The roots of the present instability lie in reactive management of gas distribution. Following the escalation of conflict in West Asia in February, the government implemented a rationing system, limiting sales to half-filled, 7.1 kg cylinders to preserve national stocks. This measure successfully managed demand for several months, but the transition back to full-cylinder sales created a sudden, overwhelming surge in domestic gas trade. As the NOC director has acknowledged in a report published in this news outlet, the announcement that full cylinders were once again available caused all previously sidelined empty cylinders to return to the market simultaneously, placing an unbearable strain on the existing distribution infrastructure. This surge was exacerbated by a lack of consumer confidence, leading to panic-driven stockpiling by households and commercial entities.

This market volatility is exacerbated by institutional weaknesses surrounding the regulation of cylinder stocks. It is estimated that there are now approximately 17.5 million LPG cylinders in circulation across Nepal, a substantial increase from the 14.4 million units verified by a 2021 exercise. Despite this massive volume of hardware, there is no comprehensive policy governing how many cylinders a single household or a commercial establishment is permitted to possess. Furthermore, no system exists to determine how many new cylinders should be released into the market annually, rendering the system cluttered and unmanageable. This regulatory vacuum enables those with the means to hoard to do so whenever a perceived shortage occurs, while citizens who possess only a single cylinder are left without any recourse.

The government and the NOC must pursue a series of robust, long-term management strategies to address this crisis. Discussions are underway to consolidate the industry, reducing the number of bottling plants from 58 to fewer than 30. Additionally, the NOC is attempting to implement more dynamic distribution monitoring by identifying specific high-demand areas and redirecting supplies on a daily basis to prevent localised shortages. These logistical improvements must be paired with clear legal limits on cylinder ownership to prevent hoarding.

While improving the LPG supply chain is necessary for immediate stability, the most sustainable solution lies in a shift towards energy sovereignty. Given that Nepal is exceptionally rich in hydropower generation, it is strategically unwise to remain heavily dependent on imported fossil fuels. In addition, the recent discovery of natural gas in Dailekh offers another cooking fuel alternative. The government must aggressively promote the adoption of induction stoves and other electric cooking technologies as a primary alternative to cooking gas. By incentivising and subsidising the use of hydroelectricity in households, the state can reduce its import bill, protect citizens from the recurring gas paradox, and leverage its natural resources to ensure a more stable and self-reliant future for every Nepali kitchen.

articles.title: What it means to be a neighbour
articles.summary:
Polarisation does not arrive suddenly. It does not even appear from afar like a procession. It comes quietly, like dampness seeping into the walls of an old house and going unnoticed for a long time. Gradually, it erodes the foundations of structures—yours and your neighbours’ too.

One day, that same neighbour at whose house you would walk in without knocking to drink tea pauses before opening the door. This pause is brief, but it is from here that society begins to change. Earlier, people knew one another’s names. They even addressed each other using terms like chacha, bhaiya, chachi, daadi. Earlier, children did not know which religion their friends belonged to. They only knew whose house had the sweetest guavas, whose grandmother told the best stories, and whose courtyard held the rainwater the longest.

Polarisation first steals away these small pieces of knowledge. Then a person no longer remains a person. They become a religion first, and their name comes later. The world remains the same, but the eyes that look at it change. The greatest victory of communalism is that it changes the way of seeing things before it burns any house.

When the gaze itself changes, the neighbour standing in front begins to feel like a distant person. Following this, a long distance is born within society—one that cannot be measured on any map. This fire, that breaks out in the eyes, sometimes takes an entire generation to extinguish.

A village or a market is not held together only by roads, bridges and government offices but by those small things for which no account is ever kept. Asking after someone’s well-being at the morning tea shop, exchanging views on some matter while returning from the fields, sewaiyan of Eid and thekuwa of Chhath reaching one another’s homes without invitation—these are the real capital of any society.

Before becoming a citizen, a human being becomes someone’s neighbour. The first classroom of social harmony is on a footpath, where children from different homes run together, where no one asks about religion in someone’s sorrow and no one counts caste in someone’s joy. Therefore, when the fire of communal tension breaks out, it does not burn only wood, tin and brick. It scorches those unspoken relationships that take years to form. The ash of the market can be swept the next day. But who will sweep the ash settled in the heart?

In Kaptanganj of the Eastern Tarai too, what likely burned first must have been that easy trust people once had—a trust so strong that for years they drank tea at one another’s shops without keeping accounts, remaining at ease knowing their children had gone to play at a neighbour’s house. But after the inferno settles, the same familiar path begins to feel a little strange. The same chowk, the same haat, the same temple, the same mosque—everything remains in its place, yet in the eyes of the people walking between them, a fine hesitation seems to settle. The breaking of society does not always happen with noise. Sometimes it happens so slowly that only the wise recognise it. They say, “The settlement is the same, but the talk is no longer as it was.” This is the greatest tragedy of any communal tension.

Nepal’s real strength has always been its diversity. Its geography comprises the Himalayas, the Hills and the Tarai. Society is made up of neighbourhoods, where relationships were formed less by religion and more by everyday life. Answers to questions were found not in religious books but in the memories of the neighbourhood. But the politics of polarisation does not like such memories. It does not want a person’s entire life. It wants only one identity. It does not see the farmers who ploughed the fields all their lives alongside people of many castes and religions. It overlooks the craftsmen whose hands built both the door of a temple and the threshold of a mosque. It only needs to know whether you are ‘us’ or ‘them’.

Those who carried many relationships within them are forced to stand in a single compartment. The identity that was once that of a neighbour—teacher, farmer, carpenter, shopkeeper, singer or friend—is reduced to a mere religious name. Our society was never as simple as politics would have us believe. There were quarrels, meetings, mixings, differences of opinion as well as partnerships. But the cart of life kept moving because shared needs, sorrows and hopes outweighed differences.

When politics draws the line of ‘us’ and ‘them’, the first thing that shrinks is that shared life. Conversations at the chaupal decrease, visits to festivals reduce, children’s games begin to divide. No announcement is made, yet the heart of society becomes a little smaller. Perhaps the greatest challenge of any plural society is that it continues to recognise its people not only by their identities but by their shared life. Because society is not made of religions, it is made of relationships. And relationships remain alive as long as someone can still call someone else a neighbour with ease.

A neighbour is not merely the one who lives next to your house. A neighbour is the one whose presence keeps alive the assurance that, even in your absence, your house is not completely alone. They are not part of the threshold of your door but are certainly part of your peace of mind.

There must have been some conditions of being a neighbour too—the sound of someone’s sorrow crosses the wall and reaches your ears. That in children’s play, the boundaries of houses are not visible.
