That when trouble is heard, the first knock on the door does not ask about religion. The history of civilisation is also the history of the neighbourhood. Walls separate houses, but neighbourliness keeps an invisible door open in those walls.

The fire of communalism first burns this invisible door. The paths remain, but trust in them does not. Even after the fire is extinguished, people continue to live in the same settlement, but it feels different. Nowadays, eyes look before doors open. Identity is checked before a greeting. Then one understands that the fire burned less wood and more of neighbourliness.

The hallmark of a civilised society is that, even in times of crisis, its neighbours can still reach one another’s doors. Temples, mosques or a strong constitution come after that. Perhaps being a neighbour is itself the first public proof of being human. The day we stop seeing someone as our neighbour and instead diminish them to just their identity, democracy will depart from both our constitution and neighbourhood.

articles.title: How emerging economies can lead with intelligent banking
articles.summary:
For more than seven centuries, banking has been built around one fundamental purpose: Moving capital efficiently across an economy. Over the next decade, however, banking will increasingly be defined by something altogether different: intelligence.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents the most profound shift in financial services since the emergence of commercial banking itself. Just as electricity transformed manufacturing and the internet transformed commerce, AI will redefine how capital is allocated, how risk is assessed, how trust is established, and how financial decisions are made. This is as much about automation as it is about augmenting human intelligence at an unprecedented scale.

Moving ahead, true competitive advantage won’t be measured by the amount of money that a bank has in its vault. It will be determined by its intellectual capital, data quality, technological capability and organisational agility.

When we look at the banking industry around the world, we notice that banks are constrained by legacy infrastructure, fragmented technology platforms and complex organisational structures. If a bank seeks to modernise those systems, it will require an investment of billions of dollars and years of execution.

Countries like Nepal begin from a different position. The country’s banking sector has the opportunity to build the financial architecture of the future rather than continually upgrading the infrastructure that exists at the moment. History rarely offers emerging economies an opportunity to leapfrog global leaders. And if adopted properly, we can actually become an example of how intelligent financial systems can accelerate inclusive economic development.

However, technology alone does not create transformation. It is the way leadership adopts and adapts to change. The organisations that will succeed will be those that are willing to break away from the traditional approaches to banking that have been carried out for decades.

For years, expansion involved the opening of more brick-and-mortar branches. But in the coming years, banks will scale by deploying better algorithms. Traditionally, banks competed with each other primarily through financial capital, but now it will be knowledge, intelligence and customer experience that will rule the roost.

This shift fundamentally changes the economics of banking. Historically, shareholder returns have been driven by balance sheet growth, prudent lending, capital allocation and cost discipline. These principles remain essential. But the next generation of value creation will increasingly come from something different.

AI will reduce operational costs, improve credit decisions, strengthen fraud prevention, enhance regulatory compliance, personalise customer engagement and dramatically increase organisational productivity. What this literally means is that intelligence itself will become an economic asset. Banks that successfully integrate AI into every layer of their operations will generate superior returns not because they take greater risks, but because they make better decisions.

That distinction is critical. However, human judgement should never be replaced by technology. Instead, we should use technology to help improve our judgement. Since the evolution of banks, trust has always been the foundation of the banking industry. And in this age where algorithms are increasingly influencing financial decisions, trust becomes even more valuable. We all need to take heed that people will not simply choose a bank because they possess advanced technology.

Customers will opt for banks that can combine technological excellence with transparency, ethics and human understanding. AI may become the engine of modern banking. Trust will remain its currency. This philosophy has guided the evolution of Nabil Bank. For more than 25 years, my father, Binod K Chaudhary, believed that Nabil should never be content with being Nepal’s largest or most profitable bank. His vision was to build an institution capable of continuously redefining banking itself.

Over the past 42 years, Nabil has consistently sought to remain ahead of structural change. From becoming Nepal’s first computerised bank to pioneering digital innovation and modern banking services, our objective has always been the same: Anticipate the future before it becomes obvious. The numbers tell part of that story.

Today, Nabil serves more than 2.5 million customers. Over four decades, the Bank has consistently ranked among Nepal’s strongest performers in profitability, return on equity and long-term shareholder value creation while maintaining one of the country’s most respected dividend records. More importantly, generations of investors have trusted Nabil to create sustainable value across economic cycles through disciplined governance, prudent capital allocation and responsible risk management.

Yet past performance is not a strategy for the future, which led us to create nBank, Nepal’s first digital banking platform developed by a commercial bank. However, digital banking is only the beginning. Our vision, our goal is not merely to use AI. We aim to redesign the bank around AI, making Nabil Nepal’s first truly AI-ready bank by 2028.

This means embedding intelligence across every major function of the institution. Every repetitive process should become automated. Every decision should become better informed. Every customer interaction should become more personalised. Every employee should become more productive. The objective is not fewer people, but better banking. AI should free talented professionals from repetitive work so they can focus on what humans do best: Exercising judgment, building relationships, solving complex problems and advising customers.

Every financial institution must ask itself difficult questions. How should AI make decisions? Where should humans always remain involved? How do we eliminate bias? How do we preserve privacy? How do we strengthen trust while embracing intelligent automation? These questions will define the next generation of banking leadership.

The future also demands a broader view of financial services. Customers expect one integrated financial ecosystem. Recognising this evolution, Nabil has expanded beyond traditional banking through digital banking, investment banking, wealth management, capital markets and fintech partnerships. Our continued investment in Nabil Invest, stock brokerage and intelligent financial platforms reflects our belief that the financial institution of the future will be an integrated ecosystem rather than a collection of individual products.

Yet technology, no matter how advanced, is ultimately only an enabler. The true purpose of banking remains unchanged. Banks finance entrepreneurs who create employment. They enable businesses to invest. They help families educate children and purchase homes. They support innovation, infrastructure and national competitiveness.

Banking will be reshaped more intensely by the coming decade than the previous 50 years combined. And it is natural that some institutions will view this disruption defensively, while others will recognise it as an opportunity to reinvent themselves. I strongly believe that Nepal should choose the latter. Our ambition should not simply be to digitise banking. It should be to build one of the world’s first AI-native financial systems.

If we invest in digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, talent, responsible regulation and innovation, Nepal can demonstrate that emerging economies need not follow the path taken by larger markets. They can create their own.

articles.title: Strengthen public service platforms amid rising public frustration
articles.summary:
Delivering seamless digital governance was one of the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s ambitious election agendas. After winning the election and assuming office in March, it set out a 100-point good governance plan that promised reforms in taxes, healthcare, agriculture and accountability to enable seamless public service delivery. Initially, it upgraded the Hello Sarkar grievance platform to operate 24 hours a day. It introduced paperless processing for passports, citizenship certificates and driving licences through the Nagarik App and cleared the backlog of smart driving licences. The emphasis on technology and digital governance in the reform agenda, along with the actions taken since assuming office in the sector, is commendable. Still, it is not doing enough to resolve the long-standing issues that hinder the country’s ambition for digital governance.

Frequent server crashes, operational bottlenecks and prolonged service outages are forcing people to navigate a complex bureaucratic maze and leave without completing essential administrative work. For instance, the Nepal Rastra Bank requires citizens to obtain a National Identity Card to open bank accounts. The government has a basic obligation to ensure that the platform to apply for it works. Yet the underlying database frequently collapses under peak traffic, creating bottlenecks nationwide. Other services that frequently go down include immigration services, passport issuance, land registration, transport management, licence renewals and tax payments.

The problem has long been ailing the public, but the urgency to tackle it is lacking. Successive governments have failed to make digital platforms work because of flawed planning and a weak system. Once installed, digital technologies require constant investment in maintenance, upgrades, patching and technical expertise and IT professionals, but governments haven’t put in the effort to keep them running, rendering them useless after a few years. Additionally, officials heavily rely on foreign technology firms for critical government systems. While there is nothing wrong with using that expertise, local workers often cannot resolve the problem independently when the system goes down. Procurement committees constantly buying cheap, short-lived systems that require long, bureaucratic delays to maintain is also creating a massive backlog for citizens. Concomitantly, with the focus on purchasing physical assets, software issues, such as their maintenance, are sidelined, leading to security vulnerabilities.

Given the widespread server crashes, it’s high time Nepal overhauls its digital systems. The government cannot continue to disregard maintenance to the point that the system completely breaks down and fails to serve the public. Any serious investment in a digital system must involve maintaining and upgrading it from the outset. The procurement process also warrants reform in line with rapidly changing technology. Moreover, rather than fully depending on foreign expertise, the government must utilise and retain the country’s young talent in the engineering and IT sector to manage critical government systems independently.

This government carries the immense trust of a public eager for reforms, which presents both a great opportunity and a responsibility to address the problems and take digital governance to a better level. It cannot afford to waste this chance.

articles.title: Exhibit review: Painting the rhythm of Kathmandu’s festivals
articles.summary:
Gallery 108 is showcasing ‘UTSAV: In the Rhythm of the Jatra,’ a solo exhibition by visual artist Pradip Kumar Bajracharya, through Sunday, August 23.

Based in the Kathmandu Valley, Bajracharya draws extensively from the region’s festivals, rituals and living traditions. His works explore how these cultural practices shape collective memory, identity and a sense of community, translating the rhythms and visual richness of traditional celebrations onto the canvas.

‘UTSAV’ brings together a series of paintings inspired by the living festival culture of the Kathmandu Valley—including the Machhindranath Jatra, Bhoto Jatra, and Sindure Jatra—as celebrated in Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Hadigaun, and other historic settlements.

Rather than documenting these events literally, Bajracharya’s work seeks to capture their essence, including the rhythm of the dhime baja, the movement of crowds, the colours of celebration, and the devotion of worshippers, translated through brushstrokes, line, colour, and composition.

A distinctive feature of ‘UTSAV’ is its formal unity—every painting in the series has been created in the same square format, a deliberate choice intended to build a sense of rhythm, harmony, and connection across the body of work.

“Art has always been a way of connecting with my culture, my memories, and the people around me,” says Bajracharya, who grew up surrounded by the festivals, rituals, and music of the Kathmandu Valley. “As our society evolves, culture continues to change. While change is natural, it is equally important to preserve the traditions and values that define us.”

Inspired by the belief that art and culture represent Nepal’s true treasures and heritage, ‘UTSAV’ is Bajracharya’s tribute to the living heritage that connects one generation with another.

UTSAV: In the Rhythm of the Jatra

When: Until August 23

Where: Gallery 108, Durbar Marg, Kathmandu

Time: 11 am to 7 pm

Entry: Free

articles.title: Indigenous voices unite for identity, rights and inclusion
articles.summary:
Marking the 32nd International Indigenous Peoples’ Day on August 9, Sunday, several institutions and indigenous communities organised events across the country, celebrating indigenous identities, culture and unity. The official programme took place at Khullamanch, preceded by a rally which started from Bhrikutimandap.

The march included several indigenous groups of Nepal, including Tamang, Kirat, Jirel, Magar, Newa, Tharu, each marching in their own traditional attire, playing instruments, waving flags, holding banners of their individual institutions while dancing and singing all together.

Queer indigenous individuals and indigenous people with disabilities were in the same procession, depicting a remarkable message of intersectional identities.

Indigenous people encompass over 35 per cent of Nepal’s population and 6.2 per cent globally. In 1994, the UN General Assembly had declared August 9 as the ‘International Indigenous Peoples Day’, marking the anniversary of the first session of the UN Working Group on Indigenous Populations in 1982. Ever since, communities from all over the world celebrate their indigenous culture, also as an advocacy for indigenous rights, and inclusive political dialogue.

With this year’s theme ‘Honouring Indigenous Midwives: Safeguarding Life and well-being’, the event was inaugurated by the Vice President Ram Sahaya Prasad Yadav. Organisers representing Nepal Federation of Indigenous Nationalities (NEFIN), the only umbrella organisation of all Indigenous peoples of Nepal, including Bimal Saru Magar, hosted the event throughout.

In his speech, VP Yadav focused on the practical implementation of constitutional rights for indigenous communities. “Inclusiveness should not remain limited to slogans but should be visible as equal access to the state’s policies, plans, resources and means,” he said.

Yadav also focused on the role of indigenous traditional knowledge and practices in promoting environmental balance and addressing climate change, calling it a model for the world. “This knowledge has today become exemplary for the whole world in addressing climate change and environmental balance,” he said.

On the role of the new generation, he suggested moving forward through education, science and technology while preserving its language, culture and identity.

Presenting indigenous identity, language, culture and tradition with pride and as immeasurable property, the event opened with a welcome dance from the Sherpa community.

Acting Mayor of Kathmandu Sunita Dangol, Minister of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation of Nepal Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, and several Members of Parliament, including Bikram Timalsina, Ram Bahadur Thapa Badal, former MP Om Gharti Magar, were present at the event along with the chairperson of NEFIN, Nima Lama Hyolmo.

Opposing the Government’s attempt to dissolve the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities (NFDIN), this year’s national slogan, ‘Protecting the rights already gained is today’s necessity. Our shared commitment is to build an inclusive and just Nepal with identity,’ laid out two distinct political messages to the assembled crowd of thousands.

According to Magar, those were: unity among indigenous peoples despite internal diversity and safeguarding the achievements gained for indigenous peoples, regardless of which government is in power.

Diversity is inevitably a matter of immense pride for every Nepali. This annual programme, which brought together thousands of indigenous people on common ground, was palpable evidence of how indigenous communities together build the nation’s cultural, traditional, and religious integrity along with ecological wisdom.

”With the recent dispute in Siraha, I had felt a surge of sadness over the country’s divided unity,” said Prakriti Rajbanshi from Rajbanshi Society Development Committee, Jhapa. “But coming here, watching all the people in their traditional attire, brought back the sense of unity altogether.”

Rajbanshi also shared the challenges of keeping her community’s identity alive in Kathmandu. While it has a strong, active presence in Jhapa, Morang, and Sunsari, where Rajbanshis make up a significant share of the population, she said it is difficult to preserve the traditions in Kathmandu. “Roughly 15 to 30 members are here in Kathmandu, and we struggle with low turnout and engagement.”

She also discussed the importance of indigenous knowledge and history, and more importantly, while acknowledging the modern world, the need to keep the traditional attire Patani authentic. “When people wear a modernised sari instead, I am simply not happy,” she said. “We should wear what’s passed down to us from one generation to the next, so that we can promote our culture.”

With individual communities’ struggle to preserve their attire, food and history, the broader indigenous rights movement in Nepal grapples with a shared set of urgent questions. “How do we bring youth back into language preservation and cultural transmission when migration and unemployment pull them away from home? How do indigenous land rights and ecological knowledge systems, built over generations, get formally recognised?”

These were the questions raised in the conversation with Sabnam Lama, President of Focus for Indigenous Girls (FIG). She explained her organisation’s role in this year’s rally, which was a joint mobilisation bringing together indigenous girls, youth and queer community under the intersectional banner.

“We wanted a diverse, intersectional message to go out collectively,” she said. “Our main work has been promoting the event, disseminating it and bringing youth together."

“Besides that, we just want to enjoy it,” she added.

Lama also spoke about intergenerational collaboration, decolonial organising and how the conversation around AI cannot be separated from indigenous sovereignty itself.

She pointed to the global expansion of AI data centres, often built on indigenous land and using indigenous water resources, as a concern that ties directly into land rights.

“When people see indigenous people, I think they should see people who are sovereign, self-governing, and who protect their nature,” she said. “When it comes to AI, we have to talk about data centres. Indigenous people need genuine, unbiased, meaningful, free, prior, and informed consent in that process.”

At the same time, Lama acknowledged that AI has become a practical tool within grassroots organisations itself, even as she cautioned against uncritical use. “In grassroots activism, we do use AI a lot—it makes urgent work easier,” she said. “Our approach is to engage critically. Ask whether it's genuinely representing us or not.”

This historic depiction of indigenous unity, knowledge, identity and collective thought, carried through traditional rhythms, conversations, songs, dance steps, was, in the end, proof that diversity and unity are a shared fact rather than competing claims.

articles.title: ‘Summer Love’ to be staged at Kantipur Theatre from Friday
articles.summary:
A stage adaptation of Subin Bhattarai’s popular novel ‘Summer Love’ is set to open at Kantipur Theatre, Gairidhara, Kathmandu, from Friday, August 14.

Produced by Kantipur Film Academy and directed by Samrat Bhujel, the play will be staged twice daily at 1:15 pm and 5:15 pm, except on Wednesdays. The production has a runtime of one hour and 45 minutes.

Actor and filmmaker Arpan Thapa is also part of the cast and will appear in the role of the writer from the novel. The actors portraying the story’s central characters, Atit and Saya, have not yet been revealed and are expected to be introduced during the premiere.

The production brings Bhattarai’s widely read romantic novel to the stage, allowing readers to see how the characters and scenes they imagined while reading the book have been interpreted through theatre.

The play marks another literary adaptation at the theatre, which previously staged a production based on Amar Neupane’s novel Seto Dharti.

“We are incredibly grateful for the love and support audiences showed ‘Seto Dharti’. We hope they will receive ‘Summer Love’ with the same warmth and enthusiasm,” said Samrat Bhujel, the director.

According to Kantipur Theatre, student tickets are priced at Rs300, regular tickets at Rs500 and special tickets at Rs1,000. Audiences have been encouraged to book tickets in advance due to limited seating.

Summer Love

When: From August 14Where: Kantipur Theatre, Gairidhara, KathmanduTime: 1:15 pm and 5:15 pm (except Wednesdays)Entry: Rs300 for students, Rs500 regular, Rs1,000 specialDuration: 1 hour 45 minutes

articles.title: Sixty years of ‘Revolver’, the album which helped The Beatles push their limits
articles.summary:
Sixty years ago, the Beatles released Revolver, an album that has a strong claim to being the group’s magnum opus. Revolver’s 14 tracks represented an unprecedented and highly innovative kaleidoscope of musical styles at the time of release and laid bare what had become an insurmountable gap between the group’s live repertoire as it existed in mid-1966 and their increasingly lofty ambitions for their output as a recording group.

Consider that just a month prior to the album’s release, the Beatles toured Germany, Japan and the Philippines on the strength of a brief setlist that still included relatively simplistic songs like Chuck Berry’s “Rock and Roll Music” and Lennon-McCartney’s own “I Wanna Be Your Man” (given as a hand-me-down to the Rolling Stones three years prior). The Revolver sessions that took place immediately prior to this tour saw the band recording music that was worlds apart from what they were able – and still expected – to perform live, in what would prove to be the final days of their career as a live act.

Indeed, barely three weeks after the release of Revolver, the Beatles performed their final commercial concert at San Francisco’s Candlestick Park. Although the road-weariness brought on by years of relentless touring was the primary factor driving the group’s decision to call time on their career as live performers, they must have also taken account of the technological limitations of the era that prevented them from presenting their extremely inventive new music to live audiences.

With Revolver, the Beatles had entered their most intensively creative and experimental era and they would dedicate the remaining three-and-a-half years of their career as a group to being a full-time “studio band” bent on pushing the limits of recording technology to realise their artistic ambitions. Revolver is a timeless album, containing unforgettable songs, uniquely “fresh” production that manages to sound contemporary even today and an audacious artistic vision that is arguably yet to be bettered.

The following is a breakdown of the album.

George Harrison opened the album with an infectious rocker that belied an unexpectedly downbeat sentiment, the Beatles’ unhappiness at being taxed at a rate of 95% – yes, ninety five percent!! – of their earnings, a result of the then-recent election of Labour Prime Minister Harold Wilson (who is name-checked in the song alongside his Tory rival Edward Heath). The group’s unhappiness at the prevailing tax rate didn’t prevent them from continuing their relentless musical innovation, with Harrison using a 7#9 chord – the so-called “Hendrix chord” – months before it was popularised by Jimi Hendrix himself and Paul McCartney playing a coruscating guitar solo influenced by Indian classical music.

Eleanor Rigby

A total change of pace from the opening track, McCartney’s sparse, desolate, yet vivid ballad about a lonely old woman completely defied expectations of pop groups in 1966, both in its lyrical theme and its musical setting; surprisingly for such a poignant piece of music, the whole composition is built on just two chords! Producer George Martin’s expertise in producing classical music proved invaluable in bringing this track to life, with an innovative double string quartet arrangement featuring stark, staccato chords that echoed composer Bernard Hermann’s iconic score for Hitchcock’s Psycho.

I’m only sleeping

John Lennon’s first track on the album conjured up an enticingly languorous mood, with its passionate defence of the simple pleasure of lying in bed contrasted with the outside world’s mechanical tendency to bustle about – ultimately, to no great end.

“running everywhere at such a speed, till they find there’s no need”

However, such a sentiment did not prevent the Beatles from continuing to innovate musically and so they did with a guitar solo by Harrison recorded normally but played “backwards,” a technique that would become a staple of psychedelic rock.

Here, there and everywhere

One of multiple McCartney masterpieces on this record, this gorgeous ballad was written in surprisingly short order when the author arrived early one morning at Lennon’s home and had to wait for him to wake up. McCartney claimed to have been inspired by the Baroque form of the Beach Boys’ recently-released song “God Only Knows,” which he would himself later rate as the greatest song ever written, but he also drew from his own bag of songwriting tricks with the bridge sections featuring a masterfully executed modulation to G-minor, the parallel minor to the song’s home key of G-major.

Yellow submarine

The album’s designated “Ringo track” proved over the years to be a timeless classic with its evocative vision of a utopian shared existence on the titular vessel. This was also the first Beatles track unabashedly intended to be a “children’s song”; this, along with the sing-along “All Together Now” recorded the following year, hinted at a “return to childhood” theme that played an important part in the emerging counterculture.

Good day sunshine

The Beatles were as adept at absorbing outside musical influences as they were at influencing others, a point well illustrated by this McCartney track, which the author claimed was inspired by the sound of contemporary group The Lovin’ Spoonful and the microgenre of “sunshine pop” which they popularised (and which reached its zenith in 1966). A pure expression of McCartney’s musical personality, which exuded a relentless optimism and zest for life, this track also deftly incorporated many of his trademark songwriting tricks, including a syncopated chorus that is in a different key to the verses, and a startling key change in the outro.

And your bird can sing

An urgent, driving rocker, this enigmatic Lennon composition is among the album’s most memorable moments, and its cryptic lyrics have encouraged much speculation about who Lennon’s subject might have been (Frank Sinatra? Mick Jagger?). Although this track is rightly lauded for Lennon and Harrison’s technically complex twin-guitar lead line, an earlier attempt at the riff using only Harrison’s 12-string electric guitar may have been the better choice in retrospect; this version of the song was likely rejected by the group for sounding too much like The Byrds and was subsequently made available on The Beatles Anthology 2 and the “super deluxe” version of Revolver released in 2022.

Doctor Robert

This catchy Lennon track’s lively rhythm complements its narrative about a co-conspiring doctor who is not averse to supplying his patients drugs (not necessarily always of the prescription variety) that promise to “pick you up” and “make you a better man”, possibly inspired by a real-life acquaintance who enabled the group’s early experiments with LSD the previous year.

Got to get you into my life

Another upbeat McCartney track featuring an irrepressible, exuberant chorus, the Beatles decided to use a full horn section on this track, perhaps inspired by R&B music coming from American labels like Stax and Motown Records; this may have inspired a sub-genre of its own, as later rock groups like Chicago permanently incorporated a horn section into their own sound. McCartney’s aggressive side as a vocalist is on full display here, but the guitar solo appears to be a reheated version of the main riff from “Paperback Writer”, released as a single a few months prior.

Tomorrow never knows

One of the biggest leaps forward ever taken by the Beatles and one of Lennon’s unequivocal masterpieces, Revolver’s startling closing track was actually the very first track to be recorded for the album.

Although the title was taken from one of the malapropisms for which Ringo Starr had become notorious within the group, the lyrics were inspired by Lennon’s own explorations of eastern philosophy (in his case, of Tibetan rather than Indian origin) and the Beatles pulled out every sonic trick that the recording technology of the time could offer, including tape loops (a forerunner to modern sampling), another meticulously-constructed “backwards” guitar solo by Harrison and Lennon’s voice being fed through a Leslie rotating speaker – originally intended for use with Hammond organs – to give it an otherworldly nature.

To this day, “Tomorrow Never Knows” retains its power to astonish and mesmerise the listener; the pioneering recording techniques have held up surprisingly well over the decades, and still sound modern. Indeed, there is a good case to be made that, even sixty years later, “Tomorrow Never Knows” still sounds like the future.
